item.title: Report: Dre Greenlaw will appeal his one-game suspension
item.description: As of now, 49ers linebacker Dre Greenlaw is not eligible to play in San Francisco's Week 6 game against Washington on Monday night.
item.content:encoded:
As of now, 49ers linebacker Dre Greenlaw is not eligible to play in San Francisco's Week 6 game against Washington on Monday night.

Greenlaw hopes to change that.

Per Ian Rapoport of NFL Network, Greenlaw is appealing his one-game suspension that was handed down on Monday after the linebacker headbutted Seattle's Ernest Jones on the sideline during Sunday's game.

Greenlaw was ejected from the contest for his actions.

This is Greenlaw's second one-game suspension in as many seasons, as he was given one last year for unsportsmanlike conduct.

Greenlaw's appeal is slated to be heard by one of the NFL and NFLPA's jointly appointed officers: Derrick Brooks, Jordy Nelson, Ron Rivera, or James Thrash.

item.title: What are your boldest takes for Bills-Rams ‘MNF’ showdown in Week 5?
item.description: The Buffalo Bills may need to employee some bold strategies against the Los Angeles Rams during Monday Night Football
item.content:encoded:
A wild slate of NFL action comes to an end this evening with the Buffalo Bills set to face the Los Angeles Rams in front of a national audience for Week 5 of Monday Night Football. Despite the 3-1 record, a lot of folks are down on the Bills at the moment, which also includes a bit of concern about quarterback Josh Allen.

Buffalo is a routine playoff contender and frequent Super Bowl favorite because of Josh Allen. Without him, the Bills resemble a lot of those teams from the drought era. It’s natural to show some concern, as much of it has to do with fans’ understanding about Allen’s importance to the team.

Yes, it’s a team and there’s plenty of room for others to make their mark. What’s said above of Allen might well stick to running back James Cook III, for example. So perhaps Week 5 will serve as a get-right game for Buffalo, if you believe they need one.

“Crazy talk,” you say? The Rams aren’t too dissimilar from the Bills as a team with plenty of firepower on offense led by an NFL MVP quarterback, but also a group that struggles to stop opponents on defense. They’re a .500 squad that’s lost to the San Francisco 49ers and Denver Broncos, while defeating the New York Giants and Philadelphia Eagles.

The Bills are marching into SoFi Stadium to take on a beatable team in Los Angeles that’s propped up by a lot of hype. There are a few things that need to happen if Buffalo’s going to exit Week 5 4-1, and for sure it has to look different than the game plan in Week 4.

Below are what I believe are some (admittedly safer) bold takes to consider. What that means? We’re not going to stand by predicting a pick-six for Damar Hamlin, or that rookie wide receiver Skyler Bell will catch the game’s first touchdown pass, which will also be recorded as the first reception of his career. You also won’t find anything laying claim to a defensive stalemate between these teams.

Instead, we’re rolling with bold but realistic takes that could be key toward getting the Bills a win and back near the head of the NFL class.

Buffalo Bills convert a 2-point attempt

It’s one of several pink elephants in the room, Buffalo’s continued struggle converting two-point tries. Ask anyone tuned in to the Bills and they’d say the preferred move is to always kick for one simply because the alternative leaves them chasing points.

For whatever reason, Allen and the offense just don’t have the right chemistry while going for two in most situations. That’s interesting because Allen has been great, historically, in goal-to-go scenarios — which is exactly what he’s faced with during a two-point try.

The go-to should first and foremost be Allen using his legs to get the points, but there’s a pair of pass catchers who make sense as the focal points in these situations. It’s all about height and hands, which is what the Bills have in tight end Dalton Kincaid and wide receiver Keon Coleman.

Additionally, and this should happen elsewhere on the field, head coach Joe Brady would be wise to utilized both running backs Ty Johnson and Cook. Each of them are major threats as receivers, while both are severely under-utilized. Any defense will be stressed having to account for Coleman and Kincaid in the paint, while Cook and Johnson operate out in the flat near the goal line, and all before spying Allen as a rusher.

It’s time to stop trying to get cute in unconventional situations. Use the guys who stand to help you the most. I have a sneaky feeling Buffalo will be forced into a two-point situation against the Rams, and they’re going to convert it.

Bills capitalize off Rams’ ST woes

The Rams field the worst-ranked special teams unit in the NFL. It’s a menagerie of awful, highlighted by a place kicker who struggles to convert points much beyond a distance of 40 yards. There’s truth to the idea that settling for field goals often leads to misery, but every point counts.

As we discussed above, the Bills are almost always better off kicking for one instead of trying for two due mainly to their own deficiencies. Conversely, the Rams may be far better off going for the first down instead of a long field goal simply because the numbers don’t favor converting the kick.

That could benefit Buffalo on Monday night, if they’re assignment sound and ready to tackle. That idea extends to the Bills’ coverage and return units. Specifically, if Buffalo can force a turnover or two on special teams, it could ignite the spark needed to build a lead the Rams must constantly chase.

Josh Allen rushes for two TDs vs. Rams

You might not believe it, but Allen is on pace to rush for 30 touchdowns this season. As a quarterback. Stop and consider how difficult it is for a full-time running back to hit 30 touchdowns in a season, then stroll back to Allen’s opportunity. Mind-boggling stuff, to be clear.

Allen doesn’t come across as a records chaser, but you can be certain more than a few people in the building have taken note of the potential feat. Admittedly, there’s no nudging necessary in asking Allen to use his legs (and feet) to claim six. He’s a natural at it, and Allen’s role as a rusher is a key part of what I like to say renders him a fire-breathing unicorn.

Almost no one wants to tackle Allen (other than Christian Wilkins), and that’s precisely why he’s so consistently good at picking up anywhere between a yard and 80 on any play. Los Angeles has probably tried to prepare for Allen’s rushing threat, but it’s difficult for most teams to replicate regardless of who mans the role in practice.

The oddsmakers at FanDuel Sportsbook tend to agree here, currently listing Josh Allen with the second-best odds (+500) to score 2+ touchdowns. This means a score via rushing or receiving. Book it: the bold take here is that Allen’s set to vulture a pair of touchdowns away from Cook this evening.

Greg Rousseau gets back in the sacks column

This one isn’t all that bold, at least beyond the idea that Rousseau is building a bit of a legendary season as a sack artist. I’ve also featured Rousseau in this space often in 2026, and that’s because of how much I enjoy watching him blossom as a 3-4 edge rusher. He spent many seasons as a guy limited by scheme, doing decent work that was lost in the shuffle.

On to the meat…

You know who isn’t all that similar to Josh Allen? Matthew Stafford. Okay, the guy is a really talented quarterback, and he’s also the defending NFL MVP. But have you seen him rush the football? Right. Stafford is not much of a scrambler, and isn’t even all that great avoiding pressure as a pocket passer.

Rousseau should get back to his newly featured quarterback-hunting ways in Week 5, perhaps notching a pair of sacks and maybe a turnover-worthy play or two in pursuing Stafford. Buffalo must make Stafford uncomfortable in the pocket to throw off his rhythm, and fortunately the defense has improved in that department under new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard.

FanDuel Sportsbook lists Greg Rousseau with the second-best odds at recording a sack (+136). So maybe it’s not too bold to say he doubles the effort.

Think you’ve got what it takes to make a play with the Buffalo Bills in 2026? Head over to FanDuel Sportsbook now and put your luck to the test!

item.title: Deep dive into the Cardinals’ trade of Marv Harrison
item.description: The when, who, why, and why not
item.content:encoded:
The Arizona Cardinals just traded WR Marvin Harrison, Jr. to the Houston Texans this past weekend. As part of the Cardinals fanbase, we have already heard this news.

Harrison was taken with the fourth overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft. Name a receiver accolade, and Harrison won that award while at Ohio State, which is known as “Receiver U.”

RELATED:IS THE HARRISON TRADE THE NAIL IN THE COFFIN FOR OSSENFORT?

Harrison was viewed as a can’t-miss gold jacket recipient. He was the next Larry Fitzgerald.

At the top of the 2024 draft, three quarterbacks were taken: Caleb Williams, Jayden Daniels, and Drake Maye. Next up, Arizona selected Harrison. They could have gotten WR Malik Nabers instead, or TE Brock Bowers, CB Cooper DeJean, or OT Joe Alt. All of these players already have Pro Bowl hardware.

Harrison’s rookie season was decent, but not eye-opening. He had 116 targets, which is a lot for a rookie. His 62 receptions for 885 yards and eight touchdown catches were acceptable. He also converted 43 first downs. Again, acceptable numbers for a rookie. But not OMG numbers from the #4 overall draft pick who had won the Biletnikoff Award as the nation’s best receiver, was a two-time All-American, and had been named the Big 10 “Most Valuable Player.”

His eight receiving TDs tied the franchise rookie record with Fitzgerald and Anquan Boldin. Again, encouraging. But he was not named to the NFL All-Rookie Team, which was a telling sign.

Then last year was a series of unfortunate events. First, in Week 6, he suffered a concussion. Then he underwent an appendectomy and missed the next two games. In Week 13, Harrison suffered a heel injury, which caused him to be gone for another two games. And finally, he had a foot injury in the Week 17 matchup with the Cincinnati Bengals. This placed him on IR. He only started 10 games with 608 yards, four TDs, but had a very good average per reception of 14.8.

All during training camp, the buzz was that Harrison was all new and would have a productive 2026 season.

Three things decided Maserati Marv’s future with the Cardinals: can’t get separation, drops, and lack of focus.   

The issues

For weeks, numerous media articles were written about not whether Harrison would be traded, but to which team and for how much equity. On the field, it had become very apparent that QB Jacoby Brissett had lost confidence in Harrison and rarely looked his way. The main reason is that Harrison just wasn’t getting open. He had issues separating himself from his defender, and Brissett threw the ball in a different direction.

Why the separation issue? College cornerbacks are not on the same level as NFL cornerbacks. Here at ROTB, we went back and researched all the corners Harrison faced in his final two years at Ohio State. That is 26 opponents, times two cornerbacks per game. Of those 52 defenders, only six are in the NFL; five played in the UFL, and one is in the CFL.

12. Out of 52. That tells us that Harrison dominated lesser talent on the rosters of Rutgers, Toledo, Maryland, Arkansas State, Purdue, and Northwestern. He had 160 yards against Youngstown State, 163 versus Maryland, 184 in the Arkansas State win, and 149 in the Michigan State game, a 38-3 Ohio State victory.

But against Notre Dame in 2023, Harrison had 32 yards, while the year before it was only 56 yards. Versus Indiana, just 18. 118 yards in the 30-24 loss to Michigan. 45 yards against Wisconsin.

Harrison has had issues with NFL cornerbacks. This is no longer college football with college football cornerbacks. And it does not help that the Cardinals are in the notorious NFC West Division, where every team’s defense is exceptional.

And then the drops. Every Cardinals fan has a memory of their most vivid Harrison drop. Ours is the sure touchdown in the loss to the San Francisco 49ers in Week 3 last year, which would have propelled Arizona to a nifty 3-0-0 record.

Against the Lions, Harrison was listed on the inactive list, when in reality, he had already been traded to Houston. Being completely healthy this year, he started four of four games with 13 targets, five receptions for 85 yards, five first-down conversions, a 17.0 yards-per-catch average, one touchdown, and one drop.

In contrast, TE Trey McBride has 56 targets. 51 for WR Michael Wilson. WR Kendrick Bourne had eight targets in the loss to the Lions alone, and 22 for the year. Brissett is simply looking elsewhere.

Last year, after QB Kyler Murray went down and Brissett took over, he connected with Wilson routinely, and Wilson had a breakout season. After the 2025 season was completed, it was apparent that Wilson had moved to the WR1 position.

The trade

According to Mike Florio of Pro Football Talk, the trade was finalized on Saturday. The Texans wanted to keep it a secret until after their game with the Tennessee Titans so that it would not become a distraction. The Texans were able to get their first win of the season with a 26-3 decision over the hapless Titans.

In his postgame presser, Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans was asked if they had traded for Harrison. He looked a bit perplexed, stalled for a second, then spewed:

“You guys want to know, huh? Yes, all right. We traded for Marvin Harrison.”

On the other side, Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur was also asked about the trade in his postgame presser versus the Lions. His response:

“I just thought it was in the best interest of the club.”

Both GMs for Houston and Arizona have a history of working together. So, the fact that Harrison ended up with the Texans isn’t that surprising. Ossenfort used to work for Nick Caserio while the two were in New England for 14 years. But this was not an Ossenfort decision; the coaching staff orchestrated this trade. Ossenfort then put the plan in motion.

Financially, it is a good deal for the Texans. Harrison is due $4 million this year and $5.62 million in 2027. He also has a fifth-year option coming up this offseason. His $22.5 million signing bonus was already paid by the Cardinals.

Harrison has been known as a dynamic receiver, just not in Arizona. In fact, out of all the productive receivers that have come out of Ohio State, Harrison has shown he is the worst of them all. Harrison does join his former Ohio State signalcaller, C.J. Stroud.

With Houston, they aren’t gambling on a rookie who hasn’t played yet in the NFL. Harrison has two-plus seasons already as a small sample. He isn’t a bad receiver; however, he has hardly been distinguished. Nobody in the league considers Harrison to be one of the best pass catchers in the league. Hell, he isn’t even the best pass catcher on his own team.

Since 2024, Harrison ranks 70th out of 130 wideouts in yards per route run (1.54) and 44th in receiving yards per game (47.8). Maybe Houston can rekindle his talent. Maybe Harrison needs to be lined up against some lesser talent on defense, eh?

Harrison just couldn’t get himself open. That is the bottom line. Yes, he had 10 drops in the 30 games he started, but while playing for Arizona, Harrison ranked dead last in the league among all receivers (with 50 targets or more over the past three years) in separation, averaging just 2.1 yards of separation when targeted, per NFL Next Gen Stats.

That is a huge stat, and very telling. Brissett just couldn’t count on Harrison getting open, so he threw the ball to the ones who were getting more than a step on their defender. And does anyone consider Harrison explosive enough? Explosive at all? Does his speed scare anyone?

It’s not like Top-10 draft picks don’t get moved. Recently, the New York Football Giants traded for QB J.J. McCarthy, who was taken with the #10 pick in the 2024 NFL Draft.

Conclusion

The question is: Did the Cardinals get enough for Harrison? A second plus a sixth just seems a bit underwhelming for a guy who went fourth overall. Plus, they could have waited until all of this weekend’s games were completed. No telling if a team like Buffalo or San Fran could have an injury to one of their starting receivers and become desperate for talent and overpay.

The big thing is that the second-round pick is for 2027, and not in 2028.

Houston’s stance is that they are taking a swing on what was perceived as Hall of Fame talent. After all, Harrison Jr.’s father is exactly that. He is still a tantalizing prospect, and he’s young enough to prove the Cardinals wrong. Texans’ fans are already pumped that he is coming to H-Town. Houston lost WR Jayden Higgins to an ACL injury during training camp, and WR Nico Collins has had his share of injuries.

Interestingly, Harrison is not going to a playoff contender. In fact, he is going from a 1-4-0 team to a 1-4-0 team.

For now, Arizona has placed Bourne in the slot and preseason darling Jalen Brooks in Harrison’s spot opposite Wilson.

Is the trade good for the Cardinals?

Well, Harrison wasn’t getting the ball and had only one season of decent numbers. Arizona fans were already on his case for the number of drops, and at the worst possible time in games. His production this year alone was horrible. His quarterback abandoned him as other pass catchers are getting the lion’s share of passes. And nobody who covers the Arizona Cardinals was talking about him.

Ossenfort needs to turn that second-round draft pick into gold for this to be a good trade.

item.title: Eagles vs. Jaguars: 8 winners, 8 losers, 6 IDKs
item.description: Let’s talk about that Week 5 loss in London.
item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Eagles nearly had this game won.

Nearly.

Instead, they’re 2-3 with the Jacksonville Jaguars handing them their third straight loss.

Time to hand out winners, losers, and I don’t knows.

For even more analysis, check out my appearance on the PHLY Eagles postgame show along with Vinny Curry, EJ Smith, Anthony Gargano, Bo Wulf, Fran Duffy, and Miles Johnson!

WINNERS

JALEN CARTER

If you’re looking for a silver lining coming out of this loss, it’s that Jalen Carter is suddenly looking healthier and more effective. That much was likely related to him wearing a less restrictive cast than what was previously necessary due to the hairline fracture in his wrist.

This might’ve been the best game of Carter’s career? If not, it’s up there.

Carter finished the day with two strip sacks (both of which were recovered by the Jags), three TFLs, and one pass deflection.

If he can maintain this level of impact more regularly, that’s a ceiling-raiser for this Eagles defense.

DARIUS COOPER

Second week in a row where his shine was stolen (in part, at least) by the Eagles losing the game. Curses!

Also the second week in a row where Cooper led the Eagles in receiving. His three targets in this game produced two catches for 71 yards, most of which were gained on his 62-yard touchdown reception.

Cooper is now up to four touchdowns on seven receptions this season. Seems pretty good to me.

Despite his success, four players had more targets than Cooper in this game. He’s a good player who deserves more opportunities. The Eagles need to be more intentional about getting the ball to him.

VIC FANGIO

The Eagles surrendered 408 yards, which isn’t great, but they allowed just 19 total points to a team that was averaging 26 points per game entering Week 5.

Additional context makes this performance more impressive:

  • The Jags’ first touchdown came after an Eagles turnover on downs.
  • The Jags’ second touchdown came on a drive that started at their own 49-yard line and was capped off by Parker Washington (who’s clearly pretty good) making a ridiculous one-handed grab in the end zone on a Trevor Lawrence fourth down throw.
  • The Jags’ game-winning field goal was scored on a drive where Fangio’s defense didn’t even take the field since Jacksonville’s kick return set up the three points with 0:01 left in the game.
  • The Eagles forced the Jags into two turnovers on downs.
  • The Eagles produced an interception and three forced fumbles. Carter’s two strip sacks both took bounces in the Jags’ favor. The other fumble occurred near the goal line and the officials determined their was no clear recovery, allowing Jacksonville to maintain possession. Going 0/3 on fumble recoveries is bad luck.
  • The Eagles’ defense faced 72 total snaps since the Eagles’ offense can’t actually sustain drives.

The Eagles almost won this game because their defense came to play. Fangio seems to be rebounding after a slow start to the season.

QUINYON MITCHELL

Mitchell is a “virgin” no longer!

Due to his previous lack of regular season picks, that’s how Fangio referred to him back in training camp:

“He still needs his first interception of his career. He’ll quickly remind you he’s got four in the playoffs, but he’s still a virgin in the regular season.“

Mission accomplished.

Mitchell secured an underthrow by Lawrence (just the third interception thrown by him this season) to bail out an Eagles offense that gave the Jags a short field to work with after a turnover on downs. Naturally, the Eagles’ offense gained 15 yards on six plays before having to punt.

Anyway, back to Mitchell, he’s been great, which is to be expected. He’s allowed just a 64.6 passer rating when targeted this season.

ZACK BAUN

Getting Baun back was a big development for this defense. He led the Eagles in total tackles with 11 and tied Arnold Ebiketie for a team-high two quarterback hits. One of those was very nearly a sack; Lawrence was fortunate to throw the ball away at the very last moment before his knee hit the ground.

Looking like a heat-seeking missile, Baun prevented a touchdown by blowing up the Jags’ final play of the second quarter:

DONTAYVION WICKS

Wicks was targeted eight times for five receptions and 63 yards. Four of those grabs resulted in first downs. He notably helped the Eagles convert:

  • 3rd-and-8 on the Eagles’ first touchdown drive
  • 3rd-and-10 on the Eagles’ first touchdown drive
  • 3rd-and-5 on the Eagles’ final drive

Wicks drew a pass interference penalty that turned 3rd-and-goal at the 17-yard line into 1st-and-goal at the 3-yard line, which set up a Will Shipley rushing touchdown.

Wicks drew another pass interference penalty that turned a 3rd-and-9 at the Eagles’ 40-yard line into 1st-and-10 at midfield.

After a strong first two weeks to start the season, Wicks was quieter over the past two games. He returned as an impactful high-leverage option on Sunday.

And he had success despite suffering a hamstring injury that kept him limited in practice on Thursday and Friday.

BRITAIN COVEY

Covey told the Inquirer that he petitioned the league to wear “Britain” instead of “Covey” on the back of his jersey for Sunday’s game. Covey’s request was denied.

Nevertheless, he came up big playing in the country he was named after by logging four punts returns for 42 yards (10.5 average, long of 18) and three kick returns for 92 yards (30.7 average, long of 42). He’s done his part this season to help give a struggling offense good field position to work with.

EAGLES FANS

The Eagles fans who made the trip to this game deserved better. They created a loud environment that gave the Jags some trouble in terms of getting the snap off properly. The Eagles’ second goal line stand was powered in part by a crowd that contributed to a false start and a delay of game penalty.

After the game, Jags players gave props to Eagles fans for making life difficult on them:

LOSERS

NICK SIRIANNI

I was prepared to say some nice things about the Eagles’ head coach!

The Eagles entered this game as 7.5-point underdogs and came very close to pulling off an upset despite missing a lot of key players due to injury.

Unfortunately, Sirianni undid any goodwill he otherwise would’ve earned by mismanaging the end of the game.

I don’t know if having Elliott kick the ball out of the end zone is the no-brainer many have made it out to be. To be clear, that was my preference because 1) the Jags didn’t have any timeouts remaining (unlike the Ravens did in a somewhat similar scenario against the Cowboys in Week 3) and 2) I’d rather trust the defense, which was playing well, than a kickoff coverage unit that was looking shakier by contrast and was also missing some regular contributors (see: an ejected Jeremiah Trotter Jr., an injured Michael Carter II).

Again, I think Sirianni made the wrong call in that spot. But I think there’s a debate to be had about his decision. It wasn’t an unconscionable choice.

What should NOT be for update: Sirianni’s poor clock management that created the situation where the Eagles were kicking off to the Jags instead of ending the game on Elliott’s field goal attempt.

Former Eagles assistant Ryan Paganetti (great follow on Twitter) outlined it well:

Sirianni is hardly the only coach who doesn’t ace game management. Look at Liam Coen! The Jags didn’t have a great day in that regard. But Coen provided value for his team with his contributions as an offensive mind. Sirianni isn’t bringing that to the table. Outside of player motivation, I’m not really sure what edge Sirianni is giving his team. Rather, he’s been a liability.

And, make no mistake, he WILL be held accountable for the Eagles’ struggles if they continue. Especially as it relates to their offensive woes:

Coming off the Eagles’ Super Bowl LIX win in 2024, Sirianni was given a mulligan for the failures in 2025. He probably won’t be afforded similar grace for 2026 if he doesn’t come up with answers.

SEAN MANNION

Let’s be clear: the Eagles aren’t as bad as they are on offense because of one person and one person alone. It’s a collective failure that largely includes Sirianni and Hurts as well. And we must acknowledge that they’re dealing with a lot of key injuries and absences on that side of the ball.

But Mannion is the play-calling offensive coordinator and the offense flat out sucks.

Here’s a bunch of numbers to contextualize their ineptitude:

Prior to the Eagles’ final drive that resulted in a go-ahead field goal, the offense had produced just 10 yards on 15 plays on their previous four drives. Four punts. They just couldn’t move the ball at all.

And the Jags have a good defense; they entered this game allowing the second-fewest points in the league. But they have allowed teams to move the ball on them; they were allowing 354.5 yards per game, the eighth-worst mark in the NFL. The Eagles mustered 232 yards against that unit.

THE EAGLES’ RUN GAME

The Eagles ran the ball 18 times for 22 yards. That’s an electric 1.2 yards per carry.

It’s understandable that the team didn’t have an amazing day on the ground. With Will Shipley getting hurt early on, they were without their top three running backs. They were starting their third-string center, their third-string left guard, and their second-string right tackle.

But was it reasonable to expect the Eagles to be at least a little bit better than this? I’d say so. Dameon Pierce showed some juice in offseason practices and he’s had NFL success in the past; it’s not like he’s a total dud.

It also could’ve been a nice time to get Hurts more involved as a runner. Perhaps that much was off the table since Hurts was listed on Friday’s injury report with a calf (though he was a full participant in practice) and he was seen riding the stationary bike between drives on Sunday. But it’s not like Hurts has given the Eagles much with his legs in recent weeks. After logging 46 yards as a runner in Week 1, he’s averaged 15.3 yards per game since then.

THE EAGLES’ KICKOFF COVERAGE

I mean, even if you want to blame Sirianni (which is more than fair), the kickoff coverage unit still had to do better than they did in Week 5. They were fortunate that the game’s opening kickoff that was returned for a touchdown got called back. They allowed the setup for the Jags’ game-winning field goal.

(Side note: How the heck is Ameer Abdullah still in the NFL?)

JEREMIAH TROTTER JR.

Seems like ejecting Trot Jr. and Bryan Thomas Jr. (how do the Jags also have a Brian Thomas Jr.?) was harsh, it’s not like he was out there throwing punches:

Still, Trot Jr. owns some level of blame for putting himself in a position where the refs made this call. Not only his absence hurt the Eagles’ special teams unit, but he was also apparently supposed to play on defense:

He wasn’t available for his team when they could’ve used him out there.

JIHAAD CAMPBELL

Campbell has struggled and that much is reflected by the Eagles planning to have Trot Jr. eat into his playing time.

ANDREW MUKUBA

Mukuba bit hard on the Jags’ play-action on Jacksonville’s first touchdown, which allowed Parker Washington to go basically untouched 51 yards to the end zone. Costly mistake.

TEAM HEALTH

The Eagles entered this game with a bunch of key injuries and they got further banged up in London. Full list here.

I DON’T KNOWS

JALEN HURTS

I’m not interested in crushing Hurts for this loss.

I’m also not interested in letting him entirely off the hook because he Left The Field With The Lead.

As previously acknowledged, this was far from an ideal spot for Hurts. His supporting cast just wasn’t very good. He had to deal with a lot of quick pressure.

But things aren’t always going to be perfect for the quarterback. And while the offensive struggles weren’t his fault alone, he was the quarterback of an offense that managed to score just three points in the second half of this game.

Again, I don’t want to crush him, because he did some really good things in this game. As was the case over the first two weeks, he carried the offense at times by making crucial completions on third-and-long. Which, as we said back then, just isn’t a sustainable way to succeed in the NFL. But he made important throws, including when he led the Eagles into range for what seemed like it was going to be the game-winning field goal.

He also missed a big opportunity to hit Wicks for a wide open touchdown. It wasn’t an easy throw with an all out blitz bearing down on him. And perhaps Wicks, who isn’t the fastest receiver to begin with (nor helped by his hamstring injury), needed to do a better job of tracking that ball and laying out for it. Regardless of who’s to blame, the play was not made, and it’s not like the Eagles had a ton of margin for error given the state of their offense.

Hurts is not the only reason the Eagles’ offense is struggling. But the Eagles paid him a lot of money to be a big reason why the offense is succeeding and that’s not what’s happening right now. He’s played well at times but they need even more from him.

MAKAI LEMON

Lemon seems to be progressing in the right direction. He set new career highs in snaps played, targets, receptions, and receiving yards in this game. Good to see!

But with Cooper coming on and DeVonta Smith coming back sooner than later, it’ll be interesting to see how the receiver rotation shakes out. I don’t know what Lemon’s role looks like then.

Also, perhaps it’s too harsh to criticize a rookie for not staying in bounds like he failed to do on the Eagles’ final drive, but him going out and stopping the clock ended up being a costly error.

WILLIE LAMPKIN

There are things to be encouraged about from Lampkin’s first NFL start:

But I also think it’s fair to say he has room to improve and isn’t yet a slam dunk long-term option by any means.

Lampkin graded out as the Eagles’ second-worst player on offense by Pro Football Focus (only ahead of Markel Bell), allowing a team-high five pressures.

I still like Lampkin’s potential. I don’t know if moving to center might help him but that doesn’t seem to be on the table with the Eagles preferring Drew Kendall (when healthy) in that role.

JAKE ELLIOTT

Elliott made what should’ve been the game-winning field goal from 48 yards out. Clutch kick.

Including training camp practices (28/31), preseason games (7/7), and the 2026 regular season thus far (16/16), Elliott is 51/54 on all kicks dating back to the offseason. That’s encouraging.

However, his final kickoff (which 1) shouldn’t have been necessary and 2) should have just been kicked out of the end zone for a touchback but he was instructed to do otherwise) was not good! The trajectory allowed Ameer Abdullah to get a running start en route to a 53-yard return that set up the Jags’ walk-off field goal.

COOPER DEJEAN

This felt like one of DeJean’s better games this season. He finished second on the team in total tackles with 10, including two TFLs. He notched a team-high five defensive “stops,” which are tackles that constitute a failure for the offense. Felt like more good than bad from him.

On the downside, he was charted with five missed tackles. That’s a lot.

DAMEON PIERCE

Pierce had 11 carries go for 14 yards. Of course, it’s not like Will Shipley was much better before he got hurt. Shipley had five carries go for six yards. I did expect to see a little more out of Pierce since he offered some intrigue in offseason practices and the preseason. But perhaps the poor run blocking left him hopeless.

In any case, we could see more of Pierce in Week 6 with Shipley reportedly set to miss multiple games and Saquon Barkley’s availability currently unknown.

A weird thing from this game: Pierce saw five of the Eagles’ 37 targets (13.5%). They resulted in two catches for negative two yards!

In fairness to the coaching staff, I suppose they realized that the Jags entered this game allowing the second-most receiving yards to running backs this season.

But, like, I don’t know that you needed to make getting the ball to your fourth-string running back, who was on the practice squad prior to this week, a focus in this game.

item.title: Joe Burrow gives stern warning to Bengals following mistake-filled win vs. Dolphins
item.description: Good enough to beat Miami, but not good enough to beat good teams.
item.content:encoded:
The Cincinnati Bengals were able to snap their two-game losing streak on Sunday, beating the Miami Dolphins by a score of 31-24.

It was nice to get back in the win column, but it doesn’t feel like anyone was particularly happy with the Bengals’ performance.

Quarterback Joe Burrow didn’t seem especially pleased when speaking to the media, offering what could be taken as a warning to the Bengals about playing complete games. Burrow noted red-zone turnovers, personal-foul penalties, and field position as areas where the Bengals fell short on Sunday.

“We got to be smarter. Two fumbles in the red zone. A couple personal fouls that hurt us, hurt our field position, gave them points on the board,” Burrow said.

Beating the Dolphins, who entered the matchup at 0-4, isn’t anything other than what is expected of a team with Super Bowl aspirations. The game never really felt like it was in danger, but Burrow clearly wanted to put the game away far sooner and in a cleaner fashion.

“We had some dumb mistakes, and we got to get those fixed if we want to be a great team,” Burrow continued.

There are a lot of good things to take away from the Bengals’ first five games of the season, but there are also plenty of things to be concerned about as the team heads into their bye week.

As the team looks to get healthy and prepare for the rest of their season, one thing is clear — the franchise quarterback is not happy with their 3-2 record, or how they got there.

item.title: Fantasy football waiver wire: 12 players to add for NFL Week 6
item.description: Injuries and byes have thinned the available player pool considerably, but there are still some useful pickups on waivers. Here are our suggested bids.
item.content:encoded:
There may be a sense of panic settling in among fantasy football managers as they look at their rosters for Week 6.

Bye weeks are starting to become a major issue with four NFL teams off in each of the next three weeks. And injuries are only compounding the depth problems. Normally, the waiver wire can ease some of the pain ... but it's not looking very helpful this week.

We're starting to see a changing of the guard (or, more accurately, changing of the lead running back) on several NFL teams. But MarShawn Lloyd, J.K. Dobbins and Woody Marks are already most likely rostered in the majority of fantasy leagues.

Desperate times may call for desperate measures.

WEEK 6 BYES: Cincinnati, Detroit, Miami, Minnesota

Fantasy football players to add for Week 6

Due to the wide variance in types of leagues and individual team needs, the players listed here include their availability rates in Yahoo leagues, which may or may not match rates on other platforms. (Suggested bid values based on $100 free agent acquisition budget for the season.)

For customized waiver wire suggestions, synced to your league, subscribe to USA TODAY Sports Fantasy's exclusive tools.

WR DeMario Douglas, New England Patriots (2% rostered)

After a terribly slow start, Patriots QB Drake Maye seems to have turned the corner. He threw for four touchdowns in a Week 5 rout of the Raiders, with two of those scores going to Douglas. Fellow wideouts Romeo Doubs and Efton Chism saw more snaps, but with Mack Hollins going on injured reserve this past week, the instant pop Douglas provided is the most important takeaway. (Recommended FAAB bid: $8)

Stream on @NFLPluspic.twitter.com/gHRSeEifXF

— NFL (@NFL) October 11, 2026

WR Germie Bernard, Pittsburgh Steelers (1% rostered)

The rookie out of Alabama had his best game as a pro on Sunday, catching six of his nine targets for 80 yards. (He also added a 4-yard rush.) Perhaps it was because he's finally starting to understand the Steelers' offensive system. But it also might just be a rash of injuries among his fellow wideouts. Michael Pittman (foot) was placed on IR and Roman Wilson left early with a finger injury. Still, Bernard filled the void when needed. (FAAB bid: $7)

TE Brenton Strange, Jacksonville Jaguars (32% rostered)

When QB Trevor Lawrence really needed a big catch on Sunday in London, he repeatedly looked for his tight end. Strange hauled in seven of his eight targets for 68 yards. He makes a solid floor play going forward if you need a bye-week fill-in. (FAAB bid: $5)

TE Pat Freiermuth, Pittsburgh Steelers (15%)

While he won't have the consistent looks and yardage that Strange will, Freiermuth is a target monster in the red zone. He snagged five passes for 44 yards and, more importantly, two touchdowns, in a win over the Colts. QB Aaron Rodgers has a history of rewarding receivers who produce; no wonder Freiermuth is tied for the position lead in TDs on the season. (FAAB bid: $5)

RB Kendre Miller, New Orleans Saints (7% rostered)

With starter Travis Etienne out until at least Week 8 and Alvin Kamara showing his age, Miller may finally be getting a chance to take over as the Saints' lead back. Though he wasn't very productive (10 carries, 30 yards), Miller did get into the end zone for the Saints' only offensive TD against the Vikings. (FAAB bid: $5)

More: Fantasy football buy, sell: 10 trade candidates for Week 6

RB Dameon Pierce, Philadelphia Eagles (2% rostered)

The Eagles backfield seems to be cursed. Saquon Barkley is dealing with hamstring issues. Tank Bigsby went on IR. And on Sunday, Will Shipley suffered a foot injury that will sideline him for multiple weeks. Pierce did rush for nearly 1,000 yards in 2022 as a rookie with the Texans, but he could only muster 14 yards on 11 carries vs. the Jaguars. (FAAB bid: $4)

RB Samaje Perine, Cincinnati Bengals (3% rostered)

Normally, a game like Perine had with 78 total yards and a touchdown catch would make him a popular waiver pickup. Unfortunately, the Bengals are off this week so he can only serve as a stash for the future. If you have the roster space (and especially if you have Chase Brown), Perine is a solid pickup. (FAAB bid: $4)

WR Darius Cooper, Philadelphia Eagles (8% rostered)

We're starting to see a pattern here. The Eagles offense has sputtered all season, but one bright spot has been Cooper's ability to succeed on deep balls. He caught another long one on Sunday, a 62-yarder in the second quarter to give him four touchdowns on the season (on just seven receptions). (FAAB bid: $4)

RB Kimani Vidal, Los Angeles Chargers (3% rostered)

I don't know what the Chargers are doing on offense either. But Vidal outplayed both Omarion Hampton and Keaton Mitchell in Week 5 with eight carries, 57 yards and a TD. If OC Mike McDaniel is just going with the hot hand, Vidal is the only one who needs gloves. (FAAB bid: $3)

WR Ryan Flournoy, Dallas Cowboys (8% rostered)

Star receiver CeeDee Lamb missed some time on "Thursday Night Football" when he reinjured his quadriceps. It doesn't seem to be anything serious, but it could result in extra snaps for Flournoy. He caught three passes for 90 yards, one of them a 48-yarder, in Thursday's loss. Pick him up as an insurance policy for Lamb or George Pickens. (FAAB bid: $2)

QB Kirk Cousins, Las Vegas Raiders (37% rostered)

With several fantasy starters set to take their bye weeks soon, Cousins doesn't have his until Week 13. If you have Joe Burrow or Jared Goff as your starter, take advantage of a great Week 6 home matchup vs. Buffalo to get your team over the hump. (FAAB bid: $2)

QB Jameis Winston, New York Giants (6% rostered)

Winston has increased his passing yardage total every week of the season. Don't expect it to happen again after he threw for 326 yards and three scores in Week 5 vs. the Commanders, but he's not afraid to put the ball in the air. (FAAB bid: $1)

item.title: Micah Parsons reportedly not expected to return from ACL tear for Packers-Cowboys game Sunday night
item.description: Sunday night's clash against his former Cowboys had been circled as a potential return date for Parsons from his torn ACL.
item.content:encoded:
Micah Parsons won't return to football this week to face his former Dallas Cowboys.

That's per ESPN's Adam Schefter, who reported Monday that the Green Bay Packers don't expect their All-Pro pass rusher to practice this week ahead of Sunday night's game against Dallas.

Parsons has been sidelined since sustaining a torn ACL in Week 15 last season. He said in August that it was "very realistic" that he could return by Week 6 to play the Cowboys, confirming reports that the Dallas game was a potential target date.

Now, that's reportedly off the table. Per Schefter, uncertainty remains regarding when he returns, but there's hope that Parsons could make his 2026 debut sometime in October.

Parsons suffered his injury 14 games into his tenure with the Packers after arriving via a blockbuster trade from the Cowboys. He had surgery to repair the torn ACL and meniscus in his left knee.

A three-time All-Pro and four-time Pro Bowler in four seasons with the Cowboys, Parsons maintained his elite form in Green Bay prior to his injury, tallying 12.5 sacks, 27 quarterback hits and 12 tackles for loss in 14 games. He was named first-team All-Pro despite missing Green Bay's final three games.

When healthy, Parsons is the anchor of Green Bay's defense and a significant part of the team's hopes to compete for the NFC North and a Super Bowl. Those hopes were dampened by a 1-2 start that featured poor offensive play. Green Bay has since won two straight games, including a 31-7 blowout of the rival Chicago Bears on Sunday to improve to 3-2 and remain on track to compete for a playoff spot.

Parsons' return this week would have bolstered Green Bay's playoff prospects. But, as of Monday, it remains unclear when Parsons will play again.

item.title: Dre Greenlaw was suspended for violating the ‘principles of sportsmanship’
item.description: Dre Greenlaw can appeal the suspension. If not, the 49ers will miss their starter for one game
item.content:encoded:
The NFL suspended San Francisco 49ers linebacker Dre Greenlaw for one game after a headbutt on Seattle Seahawks linebacker Ernest Jones:

According to the league, Greenlaw was in violation of Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1, which applies to “any act which is contrary to the generally understood principles of sportsmanship.”

Greenlaw will be eligible to return to the 49ers’ active roster on Tuesday, October 20, following the team’s October 19 game against the Washington Commanders.

Under the Collective Bargaining Agreement, Greenlaw may appeal the suspension. Any appeal will be heard and decided upon by either Derrick Brooks, Jordy Nelson, Ron Rivera, or James Thrash, the hearing officers jointly appointed and compensated by the NFL and NFLPA to decide appeals of on-field player discipline.

There was some good back-and-forth about whether there would be any further punishment for Greenlaw.

If Greenlaw was a first-time offender, perhaps he would’ve gotten away with it. But that feels like a stretch. His last name and history don’t help Dre in this instance, but it’s hard to imagine anybody else not receiving a similar punishment.

So, it’ll be Jaden Dugger and Luke Gifford against Washington. Dugger was great against the Seahawks and played like a player who shouldn’t come off the field. Gifford had some issues playing on the line of scrimmage. If Nick Bosa returns, the 49ers may be able to play their 5-man fronts without Gifford.

According to Ian Rapoport, Greenlaw will appeal the suspension.

item.title: Virginia Tech Hokies Football at the Halfway Point: What Worked, What Didn’t and Dun Busted
item.description: It’s halfway through the season and the Hokies are facing a brewing crisis. The Pitt loss was bad, but the Cal loss was flat embarrassing. Looking at what works, what doesn’t, and what’s badly broken.
item.content:encoded:
We aren’t going to dwell on the embarrassing loss in Berkeley against a banged-up Bears team. Bryan covered pretty much everything that needed to be covered. Let’s look at where the team is as a whole at the halfway point of the season, and before Homecoming.

Embarrassing: No Other Word Fit the Cal Loss

The Cal game was probably a complete bust from the mechanical delay that kept the Hokies from arriving late and exhausted, to the opening offensive effort that completely fizzled after the defense got a stop against the Cal offense. Tech struggled to move the ball beyond the Cal 40, and that persisted for almost the entire game. The firebirds will be blaming Pry for the defense and dumping heaps of scorn on John Love for missing field goals. We’ve already seen the “we’d be 6-0 if…” assertions.

Both the Pitt and Cal losses were critical hits since they are both peer teams on similar program trajectories. The reality is that the Hokies need to take into a serious advisory meeting, and some real changes are going to have to occur to salvage a winning season. It’s not the end of the world, but it is (sort of thankfully) the end of the “dark horse” CFP speculation and certainly should end the fumes of winning an ACC “Champeenship” at the end of the regular season. This team is playing for a mid-tier bowl bid, and a winning record for a change, and that is the sum total of the potential season outcome for 2026.

The loss at Cal was more of a quiet period on the end of the first half of the season where Hokie Nation had hoped to see either bowl eligibility or at least a one game push to get there. What we have now is a difficult schedule with no real certainty of any more than one additional win in the hopper. With both offense and defense sputtering in critical aspects of the schemes, it’s nearly impossible to up rate the Hokies against the remaining opponent base.

The Picture at Mid-Season

The image is not all dismal and horrid, though. The Hokies have done some good things and have some solid foundations that should allow for a pivot to push beyond a 6-game season push. The key issue is going to be whether or not the coaching staff has the confidence in the performing segments to alter the scope and pattern of both approaches to offense and defense. To do that the coaches are going to really have to sit down and concentrate on a mid-season reorganization of how they are linking and planning about games, and then how to change the pace of adjustments within them.

Build on What’s Working

There are still some really good things happening with various squads for the Hokies. If you break down the offense and defense, there are some solid performances from individuals and various rooms that can form the basis for a resurgence for the final 6 games, that could net a better paying bowl game.

The Intermediate Passing Game

Ethan Grunkemeyer is proving himself to be a solution to the current offensive woes, in conjunction with more than just Luke Reynolds as a target. The Hokie offense has established several really reliable downfield route runners and pass catchers in Ayden Greene, Que’Sean Brown, Davion Brown, and now Marlion Jackson. Both starting running backs are also very good at catching the ball, and of course Howle has collected a first-rate tight end corps starting with both Reynolds and Benji Gosnell. Ja’Ricous Hairston has also contributed scoring chops when in. The offense has proven that it can move the ball downfield rapidly and especially when there is a viable run vs. pass choice presented to the defense.

Coach Howle has to figure out a completely new set of general level game plans that make use of Grunkemeyer’s skill at operating from a moving pocket, and the strength of that receiving corps over the top, but not too far over the top. We still haven’t seen a ton of deep threat balls thrown and completed, but there have been some really excellent drive extending strikes to Greene and Q. Brown on the outer edge of the intermediate passing zone.

With the offensive line seriously banged up and struggling to get traction with its run blocking, the Hokies are going to have to push the game downfield over the top to loosen up the defense and provide opportunities for stretch and counter plays to turn Overton and Hawkins back into significant ground offensive threats.

The Defensive Line Plus…

We all heard at the beginning of the season that the defense wanted to get “natural” (four player) pressure on quarterbacks in passing situations and effectively shutting down the run. The defensive line has been inconsistent in its efforts to do the former, but very good at getting the latter completed. The reality is though that the two tackles and two ends can only do so much, and stripping the fourth player out to play max cover defense hasn’t worked. Pry needs to get back to the “bear front” of four down linemen and a run cover/pass blitzing linebacker (or extra edge rusher).

Tech finally has the size and power to stop normal runs at or even behind the line of scrimmage. It just doesn’t have the inside pressure power to overwhelm the Center and Guards in the “A-gap”, especially in must pass situations where Pry is choosing to cover out instead of going after the quarterback. He has the personnel to pull that off more often than once in a blue moon. There were several times in both the Pitt and Cal losses where the defense needed to “send the house” instead of trying to rush three and cover in a prevent. The secondary is struggling, and putting even more pressure on it by allowing a quarterback all day to throw is not going to help matters.

What’s Just Not Working

Giving the “Juniors” Better Oppornities

The Hokies have two of the best running backs in the ACC. Marcellous Hawkins, Jr. and Jeffrey Overton, Jr. are a potent combination of runners and receivers out of the backfield. The problem is that their abilities are only about 15% of the run game. The Hokie offensive line can best be described as patients in a M*A*S*H unit. The current configuration has #2s in critical positions, and the #1s might or might not be up to full speed when they get in. What’s worse is that event he #2s like Brodie Meadows are chronically down to injury. This is not just a “problem”, it’s a crippling situation. It’s one where the offensive line cannot be counted on to get a 2-yard push.

The situation really gets old fast because what we keep seeing is the continued use of A-gap Dive plays, straight blocking, and chronic wasting of early downs in running plays that are almost always failing to produce more than schedule yardage. Actually, the averages are showing that the Hokies are short of even “caveman football” four-yard gains on inside running plays. There are lots of modern names for the old-fashioned halfback or fullback dive play. The situation gets even more difficult with slow developing shotgun/pistol handoffs where the running back hasn’t even built up a few steps of momentum before being handed the ball.

It’s time for Howle to switch to a pass downfield first offense, going over the top of the defensive line on three second hot reads and tight end drags, or slot slant patterns. If he can get that sort of 5- to 8-yard play executed regularly, the linebackers will be forced to cover under the zone, and the blitzing will have to stop. That will get the running stretch and counter plays working, especially if the offense gets the pocket moving.

Once the passing game gives the Hokie run game some breathing room, the offensive line will also gain some confidence and find out what sorts of blocking audibles will work, and how best to execute those blocks. Both Hawkins and Overton are fast, cut well, and have good vision. Setting up the offensive line for success will also set the Juniors up for success.

The one big lesson to internalize is that “balance” in the offensive game plain might be weighted toward the pass for the remainder of the season. What is definitely not working is operating a stone age run-first-and-pass-in-a-panic on third and long or moderate.

The Short Passing Game Isn’t Working Either

This one won’t take long, because it’s becoming a chronic issue that will drop into “Dun Busted” unless the OC quits trying to do what plainly does not work. The bubble screens, flare patterns, and flanker screens that are completed behind the line of scrimmage fail almost every time they are attempted, especially against man coverage. The problem is that the “wide screen” is a slow developing play that depends on the shotgun and a short drop to somehow suck the defenders out of coverage and allow the quarterback to get the ball out to either a flanker or running back off the edge (usually into the boundary). If the player covering that receiver on the outside of the formation does not bite, the long slow pass is delivered behind, or at best at, the line of scrimmage with a defender draped over the receiver. Those passes just don’t develop enough of a percentage of reliable yards after catch to make them “go to plays”.

Sometimes these are checkdowns as primary routes fail to develop, but if it’s a Z receiver bail, it would be better to have that receiver downfield 3 or 4 yards or in the case of a first down attempt, the receiver should be at or beyond the sticks.

Also, please note that these are traditional screen plays where the quarterback baits the rush and flips the ball over their heads to a running back behind them, usually through the ‘A’ or ‘B’ gaps. This offense is going to have to rely on speed, not power for the remainder of the season. Speed is not defined by slow developing 20 yards soft pass plays that never complete beyond the line of scrimmage. Someone needs to write on a whiteboard in permanent marker.

ALWAYS GO DOWNFIELD!!!!

Okay, Now for the Hard Fails

There are two glaring holes in the makeup of this team that are going to continue to trouble games until someone somewhere in the organization finds solutions.

The Secondary is Going to Draw Flies

The secondary is now, officially, in the Dun Busted category. It’s been struggling all season long, but the complete meltdown giving up critical penalty yards, and then passing yardage to the Golden Bears with barely over a minute left in the game was hard to see. Yes, the officials threw a really ticky-tack flag on the play that, in the end zone for a potential Tech touchdown was not thrown when Luke Reynolds was practically tackled before the ball arrived. That’s a badly broken issue outside of the Virginia Tech program. This secondary is going to be targeted repeatedly and often for the remainder of the season, and there are several teams coming up, including the Hoos, that have capable quarterbacks and receivers.

This current secondary is not covering well. The coverage is often way too loose and a 3 to 4 second play series is slicing and dicing them like they aren’t even in the picture. In addition, when covering man on, the backs are repeatedly forgetting to get their heads turned around, and the receiver is either catching the ball over their heads, or the zebras are tossing yellow hankies about. It is true that the experience level of the players was often in question… regardless of the number of years they have been on a team, and their experience with playing with each other in coverage balance was low in the beginning of the season. Those “excuses” began to evaporate after game 4 or so. We saw a regression from the BC game through the Cal game.

Part of getting them help, is getting better at getting to the quarterback and disrupting the play behind the line of scrimmage, but the players, themselves, are going to have to figure out how to step up and play better football. The defensive secondary is probably one of the most complex tasks on that side of the LOS, and right now, this secondary doesn’t seem to be getting “IT”.

That means every team that faces the Hokies’ defense is going to target them soonest and often.

The Play Calling Adjustments Keep Going Back to Gutter Balls

“You have to establish the run.” “We are going to establish the run.” “We need to have success in the running game.” You’ve heard it, and some of you bite off and swallow it whole. That rule of offense comes from “caveman football” and it’s usually one of the first big “statements” an Offensive Coordinator/Head Coach combination makes as their hopes and dreams of going anywhere evaporate like a bowling ball dropping into the gutter before hitting the pins.

It’s really nice if you can control the clock by burning up time using the run game. Or so one would think. The simple fact remains, that Virginia Tech, with 18 seconds left on the clock moved from mid field to the 7 yard line and had enough time left to attempt a touchdown. And prior to that Cal went 75 yards to score a touchdown without running the ball.

The team that scores the most points per minute of possession usually wins the football game. If a team can score 14 points in possessing the ball five minutes, while the other team scores 7 with 10 minutes of possession, who wins the game?

Tech’s offensive coaching staff still has the urge to burn plays on snuffed runs and pass in a panic on 3rd and long. We can also add those short bubble screen thingies as running plays that fail at the line of scrimmage. The coaches need to change their thinking and base assumptions if they want to go bowling after the season is over.

The Hokie offense has proven that it can reliably go fast and downfield in the air, and that loosens up the defense for the running game to work as balance. That’s modern football, and the staff needs to fix the problem, and keep it fixed. No more getting a strike, followed by plopping the ball right back into the gutter in the next frame.

Next Saturday it’s a 3:30 Kickoff at Lane

The weather is promising to be cool and breezy. The leaves are changing and its Homecoming for the Hokies. Georgia Tech was looking shaky in the beginning of the season but just handed Duke a big defeat. Virginia Tech has a bunch to fix, and this one is a toss-up game, now.

GO HOKIES!!!!

item.title: Mike Vrabel gives updates on injured Patriots, including Will Campbell and A.J. Brown
item.description: Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel gave updates on multiple injured players on Monday.
item.content:encoded:
The New England Patriots added two more key players to their listed of injuries on Sunday. Neither left tackle Will Campbell nor running back TreVeyon Henderson were able to finish the 45-17 win over the Las Vegas Raiders.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel gave some updates on the two youngsters as well as veteran wide receiver A.J. Brown.

Patriots injury updates: 10/12

RB TreVeyon Henderson: The Patriots running back exited Sunday’s game in the second quarter with an ankle injury, and was initially labeled questionable to return. He never emerged from the locker room, however, and was ultimately ruled out for the remainder of the game.

“We’ll evaluate here and see how it looks,” Vrabel said. “Wasn’t able to finish the game and if we see that on Wednesday, he’s going to be limited, then we’ll let you know he’ll be limited. And I know that [Henderson and Campbell] will do everything that they can to get back. But unfortunately, they weren’t able to finish the game. So, I don’t know where their availability will be just less than 24 hours after the game.”

WR A.J. Brown: With Week 5 in the books, the door is now open for the veteran wide receiver to return from injured reserve. Brown originally was sent to IR after the Patriots’ Week 1 loss in Seattle due to a high ankle sprain. There has been some recent optimism about his recovery, and Mike Vrabel did not rule out a return this week when asked whether there is a chance he returned to practice on Wednesday.

“A chance? Yes, there is.”

OT Will Campbell: New England’s starting left tackle left Sunday’s game on the same drive as Henderson, and like his teammate and fellow second-year player was originally announced as questionable before being ruled out. Campbell is reportedly dealing with a knee sprain, the severity of which was determined by an MRI on Monday. His status remains to be determined, but Vrabel appeared to be cautiously optimistic.

“We’ll see how the week goes,” he said. “It’ll get looked at and continues to rehab. Wasn’t able to finish the game, so I don’t know how much time he’ll miss — if he’ll be back towards the end of the week, if he’ll be back Wednesday. We’ll take it day by day and see how he feels tomorrow, see what he does Wednesday, and keep you updated on the injury report.”

item.title: Dre Greenlaw suspended for one game
item.description: The NFL announced on Monday that Greenlaw has been suspended after he headbutted Ernest Jones during Sunday's game.
item.content:encoded:
49ers linebacker Dre Greenlaw has been suspended for one game after his actions during the first half of Sunday’s game against the Seahawks, the NFL announced on Monday.

While he can appeal the suspension, he currently will be eligible to return to San Francisco’s active roster on Tuesday, Oct. 20, as the 49ers play the Commanders on Monday night in Week 6.

While on Seattle’s sideline after a play, Greenlaw used his helmet to headbutt linebacker Ernest Jones, who was not wearing a helmet. The NFL’s announcement notes this was a violation of Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1, which applies to “any act which is contrary to the generally understood principles of sportsmanship.”

Greenlaw was ejected from the game.

Greenlaw was previously suspended one game in 2025 for unsportsmanlike conduct.

If Greenlaw appeals, his suspension would be heard and decided upon by the NFL and NFLPA’s jointly appointed hearing officers: Derrick Brooks, Jordy Nelson, Ron Rivera, or James Thrash.

item.content:encoded:
The NFL has suspended San Francisco 49ers linebacker Dre Greenlaw for one game after his actions in the team's Week 5 win over the Seattle Seahawks.

The league announced his suspension on Monday. Greenlaw intends to appeal the decision, NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport reports.

According to the league's press release, Greenlaw "used his helmet to headbutt Seattle linebacker Ernest Jones IV, who was not wearing a helmet, violating Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1, which applies to "any act which is contrary to the generally understood principles of sportsmanship.'"

Greenlaw was flagged for hitting Sam Darnold late when the quarterback was running out of bounds. It happened on the Seattle sideline, so the Seahawks came to their quarterback's aid.

Jones confronted Greenlaw and appeared to push the 49ers linebacker's facemask.

SAM DARNOLD IS HIT LATE AND THE SEAHAWKS BENCH IS NOT HAPPY pic.twitter.com/pJvPtuUgQ2

— ClutchWire (@ClutchWireHQ) October 11, 2026

Greenlaw responded by headbutting Jones, who was not wearing a helmet.

Greenlaw was ejected after headbutting Jones on the sideline pic.twitter.com/N8M1ucPWfD

— Billy M (@BillyM_91) October 11, 2026

Replay caught the action, and it was reviewed. According to the postgame pool report, the league used its new rule, under which the Art McNally Gameday Central in New York can eject a player even without a flag being thrown. This stemmed, in part, from DK Metcalf's interaction with a fan last year.

The review cited Greenlaw for non-football conduct, and he was ejected for the rest of the game.

If the linebacker doesn't appeal, he'll serve a one-game suspension for San Francisco's Week 6 matchup with the Washington Commanders on Monday night.

This isn't Greenlaw's first ejection. He first got the boot after a helmet-to-helmet hit on Los Angeles Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert. Greenlaw then made headlines after Philadelphia Eagles chief of security Big Dom confronted him, and the linebacker shoved his face before getting ejected.

Greenlaw was suspended for one game in 2025 after he confronted and "verbally threatened" referee Brad Allen following a loss. The linebacker was fined for taunting earlier this season after repeatedly exchanging words with the Denver Broncos' sideline and head coach Sean Payton after Denver released him earlier this year.

item.title: Fernando Mendoza gets his feet wet in live action
item.description: It was a cold and rainy day at the tail end of a blowout when Fernando Mendoza got his number called for the Raiders.
item.content:encoded:
Fernando Mendoza, the Las Vegas Raiders 2026 #1 overall pick, saw his first live action of the regular season. At the end of a 45-17 blowout to the New England Patriots, Mendoza was brought in to run the no-huddle offense for a series. Watching him come in and go through his progressions, make the correct reads and good throws should remind us of something ‘The Sheriff’ once said.

“I learned a lot of good football at the end of bad football games.” – Peyton Manning

Sure, it was garbage time and the Patriots had called off the dogs. However, even when the Patriots dialed it up once Mendoza and the offense ventured into plus territory, he proved up to the task. Mendoza showed some escapability and a willingness to tuck it and run when there wasn’t anything downfield.

Every pass delivered had some zip on it and none of the wideouts dropped a pass he threw. His first five passes were all accurate completions to four different receivers. His sixth pass was caught, but Malik Benson couldn’t get his second foot down in bounds. His seventh pass was broken up by Elliott Davison, who sat on the out route and waited for him to throw out when the blitz rushed his throw.

It was a good outing for Mendoza. Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak was quick to tell reporters that it didn’t signify a change in the plans for which quarterback would be starting moving forward. It’s still Kirk Cousins’ job, but an opportunity to get reps for his young signal caller presented itself and he took it. It was a small sample size of things to come, but definitely cause for excitement.

item.title: Fantasy football buy, sell: 10 trade candidates for Week 6
item.description: Whether you're 5-0 or trying to save your fantasy football season, there are plenty of trades to make in Week 6.
item.content:encoded:
Being 5-0 or 4-1 in fantasy football is so much fun. You've had a great last month of Sundays and are feeling good enough about your spot in the playoffs that you can do some long term roster planning. One easy way to do that – buying into a bye week.

Week 6 is the first time this season that four teams are on bye, which means that some teams are going to really feel a roster crunch. If you're in a good spot and one of the 0-5 or 1-4 teams in your league has a buy target on the Bengals, Lions, Dolphins or Vikings, consider trading them a player or two with good matchups this week for one of their stars on a bye. Use the standings to your advantage and create some trades that help the bottom feeder in the short term and you in the long term.

With that said, here are 10 fantasy football trade targets for Week 6:

Week 6 fantasy football players to buy

RB Woody Marks, Texans

We'll start with an obvious one. David Montgomery has been terrible for a month and then injured his groin in Week 5 and could miss time. Marks was good, not great with a big workload as a rookie, but Houston has since added Kayshon Boutte and Marvin Harrison Jr. at wide receiver. The upgrade in field stretching will make Marks a locked-in RB2 when Montgomery is out and potentially even for the rest of the season.

WR Devaughn Vele, Saints

The Vikings defense is blanketing the NFL and New Orleans was the latest victim in Week 5. Vele did not have a good game, but neither did anyone else, and he still tied for the team in targets (six) and catches (four). Try and buy low on the Saints current WR2 before a get-right spot against the Giants in Week 6.

TE Harold Fannin Jr., Browns

The second-year tight end finished with one catch on four targets against the Jets in a monsoon. It's really hard to throw and catch a soaking wet football. If the Fannin manager wants to sell low, worst case, his value should be higher in two weeks after playing the Ravens and Titans.

WR Luther Burden, Bears

Simple thought process: If a team's WR1 just played with two QBs who combined for 165 yards and three interceptions but is now on the cusp of getting their star QB1 back, you should buy low on that player. Burden has been serviceable without Caleb Williams and it seems unlikely he gets worse once Williams returns, which could be Week 6.

TE George Kittle, 49ers

If Deebo Samuel is hurt and misses any time, you might be playing wide receiver for San Francisco next week. It is getting bleak out there. Kittle had just five catches for 24 yards against the Seahawks but should return back to overall TE1 consideration over the next month with very little target competition against the Commanders, Falcons, Raiders and Cowboys.

Vikings DST

This is only for the top tier of fantasy rosters, as Minnesota is off this week and holding two defenses is rarely the right move. Especially when the Vikings come out of the bye to play the Colts, Lions, Bills, Packers and 49ers. And yet ... this Minnesota defense is top 3 in just about every category you care about. They get the Commanders and Jets in Weeks 16 and 17 to end the fantasy season. If you're comfortably making the playoffs, think about making this unconventional move.

More: 12 instant fantasy football takeaways from Week 5

Week 6 fantasy football players to sell

RB Jaylen Warren, Steelers

I'm a huge Warren fan – he leads Pittsburgh in both rushing (410) and receiving (230) yards – and don't put him on the sell list lightly. This is also the kind of move you should only make if you're packaging Warren and another player to get someone like Kenneth Walker or Derrick Henry. But if you can tier up, Warren has to deal with Rico Dowdle coming back to split the backfield as early as Week 6 and is probably going to have a decrease in carries.

WR Dontayvion Wicks, Eagles

Wicks had a solid five catches for 63 yards in London against the Jags, though it was without DeVonta Smith. Once Smith returns from a hamstring injury, Philadelphia might not be healthy enough on the offensive line (or anywhere else on offense, really) to support two pass catchers.

RB Bucky Irving, Buccaneers

Don't let Irving's huge "Thursday Night Football" of 21 carries/165 rushing yards/two total touchdowns distract from the Cowboys having potentially the worst rushing defense in the NFL. Tampa Bay has two other running backs (Kenneth Gainwell and Sean Tucker) who are always lurking to take away touches and has also been a mess offensively. If you can get someone excited about the eventual return of Baker Mayfield despite his dislocated thumb, maybe you can get a RB1 return for Irving.

QB Jacoby Brissett, Cardinals

The 33-year-old veteran has been the king of garbage time and an absolute delight as a late-round QB dart in fantasy. On Sunday, he ripped out three touchdowns and 292 yards on 47 pass attempts in a 45-21 loss to Detroit. However, the Cardinals are 1-4 with a putrid -54 point differential. It's a matter of when, not if, they go to third round rookie Carson Beck just to see what they have. Get something in return for Brissett while you can.

item.title: 3 lessons we learned from the 49ers’ win over Seattle: The bullies are back
item.description: The 49ers took it to Seattle and sent a strong message
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers punched, got punched, and punched back on their way to their fifth consecutive victory in 2026 with a hard-fought, message-sending win over the defending Super Bowl champions. From the first play, the 49ers were hell-bent on sending a message: the bullies are still here, and last year was last year. The team survived a momentum swing in Seattle’s favor and responded with two consecutive scoring drives to take a lead they would not relinquish. The pass rush was ferocious, and with Nick Bosa’s return imminent, this defense feels on the brink of truly breaking out.

Here are three takeaways from the 49ers’ massive win over Seattle:

Mike Evans is a Hall of Famer

Not that his status was ever in doubt for a gold jacket, but the veteran receiver was the best player on the field on Sunday. When the chips were down, Brock Purdy targeted Evans often on a drive punctuated by a Brandin Cooks touchdown grab and a two-point conversion from Evans. Routinely whipping Josh Jobe, Evans made contested catch after catch, and Purdy’s rapport with the veteran looked like a ten-year relationship.

Evans leads all wide receivers with 11 first downs on third down. The 49ers needed speed and separators at the receiver position to test Seattle’s secondary. On Sunday, Evans dominated and didn’t even need any separation. Age ain’t nothing but a number! Way to go, Big Mike!

The 49ers’ running game sends a message

Seattle’s defense is fast and physical and can slow down outside zone runs. What is the answer? The 49ers went back to bully ball and beat up Seattle with their interior offensive line and duo runs. Christian McCaffrey finished with a 6.2 YPA and two runs over ten plus yards.

According to Sumer Sports, the 49ers’ run game produced the highest designed rush success rate in any game against a Mike Macdonald defense. They had an 80% success rate on outside zone and had 3.1 yards before contact on those runs. The Seahawks’ previous opponents averaged 0.7 yards before contact on outside zone.

The final drive leading to the leading field goal was a complete statement on the ground. The bullies are back, and the 49ers can play any style you like to finish a victory.

Renardo Green has arrived

The 49ers defense had many stars on Sunday. A monster game from Gracen Halton, another classic Fred Warner performance, and a pass rush highlighted by Keion White, Sebastian Valdez, and the returning Mykel Williams all need to be discussed. Malik Mustapha was physical and flying to the football. Even with Dre Greenlaw’s ejection, the 49ers defense was flying around, and Raheem Morris is doing a fantastic job as the defensive coordinator.

It was Renardo Green who may have made the loudest statement on Sunday. Two interceptions and a PBU while allowing two catches for five yards and an NFL QB rating of 8.3 is truly elite play. Even facing the best receiver in the NFL was no issue for Green, as the Florida State cornerback held JSN to one catch for four yards on three targets with an interception and a PBU.

Green has three interceptions this season and is blossoming before our eyes.
