WR Tre’ Harris – 69.8
TE Charlie Kolar – 66.0

Welcome back, Scott Matlock!

After returning from IR and making his season debut, Matlock turned in the Chargers’ highest grade on offense. He excelled as when used as an extra pass protector (his 82.5 grade led the team) while also earning a run block grade of 70.2 (5th best). His best play of the day came on Kimani Vidal’s 42-yard touchdown run where Matlock hauled himself down the field to throw a key block alongside receiver Theo Wease.

Of the four rookie offensive linemen who started Sunday’s game, Burke performed the best and graded out as the offense’s third best player. He unfortunately allowed a sack and ended with a porous pass block grade (39.7) but was outstanding in the run game (84.2).

Harris’ injury hurt the Chargers’ run game after he was forced to exit the game. Before going down, he had the team’s third-best run block grade at 81.6.

Worst

QB Justin Herbert – 41.8
OG/T Logan Taylor – 44.0
TE Oronde Gadsden II – 44.7
OG Cole Strange – 50.1
C Jake Slaughter – 51.6

Taylor ended up being the worst-graded rookie offensive lineman against the Broncos. It was a shock that the Chargers put Taylor at guard when he had mainly played tackle in the preseason, on top of putting Harkey at riht tackle after he played mainly at guard in the month of August. Either way, it was a rough outing for Taylor who finished with a 31.9 in pass pro.

Many of the tight ends were used as extra pass protectors and Gadsden somehow finished with an actual 0.0 in that category.

Not a surprise that Herbert was the offense’s worst. His pick was ugly and his production was one of the worst he’s ever had in his career on top of yet another lost fumble.

Defense

Best

LB Del’Shawn Phillips – 89.9
EDGE Akheem Mesidor – 89.6
EDGE Bud Dupree – 85.4
LB Daiyan Henley – 75.4
S Elijah Molden – 69.9

Earlier Monday morning, Phillips had an elite 90.0 game grade. After checking back while typing this up, it changed to an 89.9. I don’t know what the change came from, but Phillips deserved his first elite game at linebacker even in a loss. He had run defense and tackling grades above 80.0 and the team’s second-high coverage grade at 77.3. All while playing the second most snaps among defenders.

Mesidor earned the Chargers’ only sack of Bo Nix and later helped force a fumble when he hogtied Nix before Tuli Tuipulotu punched the ball loose.

Henley was in his bag as a coverage player, earning the team’s highest mark at 85.1. His 79.4 in tackling was also second best.

Worst

S Genesis Smith – 35.5
LB Marlowe Wax – 36.5
DT Nick Barrett – 44.8
DT Teair Tart – 47.9
S Tony Jefferson – 49.5

It continues to be an up-and-down rookie season for Smith. Just two games after being the highest-graded player in all of Week Three, Smith ended Sunday’s game with the lowest grade on the entire team. His 36.7 coverage grade was the worst on the defense by a wide margin and he was given fault for allowing Courtland Sutton to go untouched and uncovered for the Broncos’ fourth-quarter touchdown.

Jefferson’s 49.5 in coverage was the next worst coverage grade on the team. The roughing the passer penalty called on him (should not have been flagged) also dropped his grade a bit this week. Otherwise, Unc was fairly solid with grades above 63.0 in run defense, tackling, and pass rush.

item.description: The Eagles were able to bring back Zion Wilson to the practice squad.
item.content:encoded:
Back from London, the Eagles will need to make several roster moves this week to account for injuries and significant depth issues. One of the first spots to be filled is on the practice squad, with the team re-signing interior defensive lineman Zion Wilson.

Wilson was with the Eagles for some of the summer, signing as an undrafted free agent in June 2026 after playing his collegiate career at Eastern Carolina University. He tried to play one more season for the University of Virginia, but the NCAA denied his waiver for additional eligibility.

Here’s what BGN’s Brandon Lee Gowton had to say about Wilson several months ago:

“The 6-3, 316 pound Wilson originally played offensive line for ECU with his first game action being a mere three snaps at right guard in 2023. He transitioned to defensive tackle in 2024, where he logged 13 snaps, in addition to playing an occasional fullback role. Wilson finally became a full-time player in 2025, producing 42 total tackles, 10 TFLs, seven sacks, and one pass deflection in 454 defensive snaps played.

Wilson might’ve become a draftable player had he been able to play for Virginia this upcoming season. Instead, he joins Eagles in an uphill battle to make the 53-man roster. Making the practice squad would be a good outcome for him so that he gets more time to develop.“

It took a few months for Wilson to get a spot on the practice squad, but he’ll give the Eagles a fresh option.

item.title: Should the Rams have made a bigger push for Mike Evans?
item.description: The Rams should have targeted Evans instead of Jaylen Watson
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Rams had a hectic offseason by adding Trent McDuffie, Jaylen Watson, Myles Garrett and drawing Aaron Donald out of retirement, but now with hindsight, should the Rams have made more of a push for Mike Evans? The 33-year-old receiver is having a resurgent season with the San Francisco 49ers and may have been a more valuable addition than one of L.A.’s other signings.

The Rams could’ve avoided Jaylen Watson, added Mike Evans

Evans and Watson both signed deals with their new respective NFC West teams before the start of the 2026 season.

Watson signed his three-year $51 million deal, and he’s been solid for the Rams, but he missed Week 4, and hasn’t been as dominant for the Rams as Evans has been for the 49ers.

Evans signed a three-year $42 million deal, and has looked as great as he ever has with 24 catches, 300+ receiving yards and three touchdowns to go along with 5 wins. He’s been everything the 49ers could’ve hoped for and more.

The Rams added Watson, while Evans ended up on the 49ers

In defense of the Rams, they already had Puka Nacua and Davante Adams for 2026, and it was their defensive unit that they chose to retool over their offensive one. This made sense given the offense retained the bulk of its stars.

But with hindsight, perhaps Sean McVay and Les Snead should’ve considered adding Evans and unleashing what could’ve been a top offense with the depth to handle missing either Nacua or Adams with Evans in the fold.

Of course, Adams has been tremendous so far for L.A., but wouldn’t the Rams be better with Evans also in the mix? It’s a fair question.

The Rams weren’t wrong adding Watson

The Rams weren’t wrong adding Watson. No one should be saying that in the first year of his deal, but one can wonder if Evans would be doing more for the Rams and their ability to win football games than Watson?

It’s fair to wonder with the power of hindsight if the Rams let one of the biggest free agent weapons of 2026 go to their division rival. And now it’s fair to wonder if Evans will be helping the 49ers win the NFC West, while the Rams fight for a playoff spot.

Of course, in a few weeks we could be saying that Watson was absolutely the right move for L.A. Perhaps Evans never wanted to go to L.A. We’re speculating here.

Call it hindsight, call it preference and or perception, but one could argue the Rams should’ve made more a push for Evans over Watson in 2026, whether that’s actually true or not.

One could argue the Rams should’ve ignored Donald wanting to come out of retirement, and instead used his guaranteed money to try and lure Evans.

It’s all fair speculation.

What’s not speculation is the 49ers are 5-0 since signing Evans. The Rams are 2-2 since all their offseason signings. L.A. will look to rise to 3-2 on Monday Football against the Buffalo Bills or fall to 2-3.

Evans and the 49ers will be watching.

item.title: Colts have more questions than answers
item.description: We need better out of both to succeed.
item.content:encoded:
When watching games, I generally only have three or four things that I think are relevant enough to mention and I know that sometimes those overlap with what colleagues have written, or members have posted. My list is longer this week, containing at least nine bullet points that I’d like to bring up and discuss. So, in no particular order, here are a bunch of things that caught my attention vs the Steelers.

John Madden famously said that “If you have two QBs, you have none.” Well, what if you have five LBs in a system that only uses two? If Davis-Gaither, Carlies, Ajiake, Boettcher, and Allen are all finding their way on the field, just answer me why? Sure, they are all basically new to the system, but are you trying to get the right guy for each situation? I’ll be honest, I was in favor of moving on from Franklin. I did sort of think we would retain Pratt to have a veteran presence. In short, it is a bad unit, that lacks the instincts of good NFL LBs.

The LB woes lead right into the next observation/gripe in that you can’t win if you do not tackle. Old timers will tell you the basics of the game are blocking and tackling and it holds water. The tone was set on Warren’s (theirs) 80 yard reception. A missed tackle by Boettcher and no interest in taking on Metcalf, let alone the ball carrier in the secondary, saw him nearly untouched. Bad angles, arm grabs and trying to bump someone down is just too common of an occurrence. In my humble opinion, tackling is nearly 100% effort, and it looks we are gave about 50%.

If blocking and tackling are the basics, I thought we pass blocked well, but what is wrong with the run blocking? JT is obviously a great RB, so why hasn’t he gained 100 yards in game, since London last year? There has been some mention made of playing from under center more, but those attempts did not go well either on Sunday. I am going to speak the blasphemous, by saying that JT’s “patience” that he is famous for, sometimes needs to be changed to hitting the hole that has the best chance of being there, and hitting it quickly.

My note of the pass blocking being sufficient, brings to light another concern. We had a cleaner pocket, but still many passes were from retreat mode, rather than stepping into the throw. I know it is necessary sometimes and you can’t be a great QB if you do not have that backfoot throw in your arsenal. Still, you are going to complete far more of the ones that you set, then drive to your target. If you don’t have the confidence to do that, maybe you should sit until you do. I’m not suggesting a QB controversy, but more asking DJ to take a look in the mirror and ask himself if he is ready.

I haven’t seen snap counts, but I think we were heavy in TE usage most of the game. We did manage to get it to Mo twice and Ogletree once, but if you are going to have them out there, they need to be targeted more, otherwise just bring Tenuta in. You are running a lot of short routes anyway, so make defenses be aware of their existence. They have proven capable of making the catch when thrown to. If they simply have to be there in order to have any protection at all, then you have a different problem.

The D wasn’t good and I will point to a lack of confidence in Lou that I have written about in the past, and agree with Andrew Aziz’ call for his removal as DC. I will just ask you this, are you confident that you will make a team punt when you back them up with a hold on first down? You should be able to stop a team from gaining 20 yards in three downs. Hell, the game is about stopping them from gaining 10. I have little to no confidence that even when our opponent is well behind the sticks, that we can make them give up possession. We’ve picked off one pass and recovered one fumble over five games.

My last three concerns are Shane related. If you are consistently settling for FGs, then your play calling is not aggressive enough. Not necessarily going for it instead of taking the points, but not putting receivers past the sticks on 3rd down. I thought he displayed a sort of killer instincts at the beginning of last year, but that appears to have been the exception, rather than an improved philosophy. There is no aggression in his play calling and he is too happy trying to call plays that keep them in FG range, rather than extending drives.

Speaking of aggression, Burkes needs to be on the field far more often. He has shown the ability to get behind a CB. If he beats a couple of them, the Safety has to honor it. I want to see if he has that ability to go up and get it. He’s got some strength and vertical jump, so he needs the same kind of targets that Pierce got as a rookie. Remember, he got 12 starts and 78 targets as a rookie and even though we thought he ran a ton of empty fly routes, he did stretch the field.

My last Shane rant goes to our last gasp yesterday. Down two scores with just over six minutes in the game, you get a decent gain on first down and you huddle? Jones has been in the league and under center for long enough to run this requirement for anyone who plays the position. Shane needed to relinquish control at that point and needs to do it for some series during the game as well. We all saw Rivers command an offense and a team of strangers, with a tryout and two practices. He did this with no mobility and limited arm strength. Shane needs to give Jones the same freedom.

You might ask why I appear to be giving Ballard a pass. My thought is that he has made his bed and nothing he does for the remainder of this year, will affect his job. If the coaches that he chose can’t get enough out of the players he chose, he will be looking for work. It does bring to my mind a thought, which my wife says is dangerous, but if player development is as difficult as it appears to be, maybe you need to use all of your draft picks on established players? The biggest benefit of a rookie is his control and contract. Why not trade your unknown for a known commodity?

I read a nice piece on The Feed, from Natural Born Buddha called “Some Thoughts”. I found it hard to disagree with much of what he shared and even though we overlap a little, there are some different views on similar observations. Give it a read, I think you will enjoy it.

item.title: 3 things we learned from the Bengals’ bounce back win over the Dolphins
item.description: The offense is alive and well.
item.content:encoded:
Don’t look at the final score. The Cincinnati Bengals (3-2) were in control against the Miami Dolphins (0-5) from start to finish, despite giving up some garbage time points.

Here’s what we learned from the 31-24 win.

The running game has hope

The loss against the Jacksonville Jaguars was a heartbreaker in a lot of ways, but one of the biggest issues was the complete absence of a running game.

Against the Dolphins, though, the Bengals rushed for a season-high 117 yards.

A big reason was the performance of Samaje Perine, the ultimate team player, always ready to step in when called upon.

Perine got 68 yards on 14 carries and also had a receiving touchdown.

What’s really encouraging is that the run game was pretty consistent, as those 117 yards came on 31 carries, with neither Perine nor Chase Brown nor Joe Burrow having a run longer than 11 yards. The Bengals just steadily wore down Miami’s front seven.

Jordan Battle has a lot of pride

Say what you want about his tackling or revealing Malik Willis’ tells before the game, but Battle backed it up with interceptions on back-to-back drives, the first such performance since Dre Kirkpatrick back in 2014.

Battle also had a couple of big open-field stops in the run game. He’s showing what he can do in spurts. Now he just needs to be more consistent.

Yes, the run defense against Miami was very bad (allowing 217 yards on 34 carries), but, to be fair, they were playing in brutal weather conditions- the hottest road game in Bengals franchise history. Players were reportedly getting IVs on the sidelines.

So there’s hope that Battle and the rest of the run defense will be even better after the bye.

Special teams are going to be the focus of the bye

This is not acceptable anymore. The muffed punt and roughing-the-punter penalty in Week 3, then a roughing call that turned a Miami field goal into a touchdown on Sunday.

Special teams mistakes are really hurting this team.

These are simple fixes, so expect Darrin Simmons, the longest-tenured coach on the Bengals, to get his unit in order over the bye week.

item.title: Nick Sirianni's mistake was confirmed by his kick-coverage unit
item.description: Eagles coach Nick Sirianni took the blame for the failure to put the final kickoff of Sunday's London game against the Jaguars into the end zone.
item.content:encoded:
Eagles coach Nick Sirianni took the blame for the failure to put the final kickoff of Sunday's London game against the Jaguars into the end zone. And, yes, it would have made sense to put the Jaguars on their own 35 with no timeouts and eight seconds to play.

The other part of Sirianni's admission is that he knew he shouldn't have trusted his kick-coverage unit to make a tackle. Indeed, the game started with a 90-yard kickoff return for a touchdown by the Jaguars that was nullified by offsetting penalties.

As former Steelers coach (and possibly future NFL coach) Mike Tomlin said during Sunday night's coverage of Ravens-Falcons, a coach needs to be able to trust the players on the back end of the roster to perform on special teams. Sirianni's certainty that he should have called for a kickoff into the end zone contains an implicit concession that he shouldn't have trusted his kick-coverage unit to deliver in that moment.

Which raises a real question about the overall quality of the roster. Do they have enough players who can be relied upon to make a tackle on an important special-teams play? Based on what happened on Sunday, they don't.

Complicating matters is the fact that they apparently plan to devote one of their 53 roster spots, for the rest of the season, to retired right tackle Lane Johnson as part of a strategy to defer the bulk of his cap charges in 2028. That makes it harder, not easier, to have enough competent players to make the play that wasn't made on Sunday.

Which brings it all back to the kickoff decision. Sirianni is convinced he made the wrong call. And the outcome proves his point.

item.title: Marvin Harrison Jr. trade: Fantasy football impact for Texans' Nico Collins, C.J. Stroud and more
item.description: Hayden Winks examines the fantasy fallout of Marvin Harrison Jr. joining the Texans.
item.content:encoded:
The Marvin Harrison Jr. trade to the Texans was confirmed by head coach DeMeco Ryans himself after the team's blowout win against the Titans. Houston is sending a 2027 second-round pick (currently 39th overall) for Harrison, with Arizona also moving up from the seventh round to the sixth round in a pick swap in the 2027 NFL Draft. 

Here are the WRs to be drafted in the second round in the last three classes for reference: De'Zhaun Stribling, Denzel Boston, Germie Bernard, Jayden Higgins, Luther Burden, Tre Harris, Jack Bech, Keon Coleman, Ladd McConkey, Ja'Lynn Polk and Adonai Mitchell.

Harrison may not be the very best of this group moving forward, but he's certainly better than many of them. Ultimately, the trade compensation is within the range of normal, even if there are very clear pros and cons to his game. I wrote about them extensively over the weekend as well as the fantasy fallout for the Arizona Cardinals. Now, let's dive into the fantasy ramifications for his new team.

Texans Fantasy Fallout

The Texans absolutely should be a pass-first team. If we stacked every team's offensive success rate on passing and rushing plays, the Texans are 13th in passing and 63rd out of 64 units rushing, only ahead of Browns' run plays. This isn't a new problem either. It's been the worst rushing team since CJ Stroud and Ryans have been together. A David Montgomery groin injury should unlock Woody Marks to some degree, but the RB and OL talent are nowhere near fixable in 2026, when the Texans are fighting off a 1-4 start with a clear-cut contender in their division. 

Stroud can handle a pass-first offense, at least when Nico Collins is healthy. Stroud's +0.16 EPA per play with Collins on the field is QB5, only trailing Jared Goff, Josh Allen, Brock Purdy and Dak Prescott. When Harrison takes snaps away from Xavier Hutchinson and Kayshon Boutte, then they can become even more potent. They are also clearly better when 2025 third-round slot WR Jaylin Noel is playing the appropriate amount of snaps.

Collins is half PPR's per-game WR4 on WR8 usage. His 105 air yards are WR9 and give him long-TD ability, and he's easily the top red-zone threat on the team. The downfield role is unlikely to change for him with Harrison around. Collins will likely eat the most snaps at X receiver, which typically means a well-rounded but vertical-built route tree. The Cardinals tried Harrison in that exact role, and it straight-up failed due to a lack of speed. Collins is one of the rare WRs who can be given the most difficult route assignments and still produce like one of the best. If there's an area of the field that could get a bit squeezed with Harrison around, it's in the red zone, as his big frame could be viewed as a first-read asset. It's enough to knock Collins down a hair in rest-of-season rankings — I'd take Collins WR10 if drafting today — but this should not be viewed as a 1A/1B situation. Collins is simply on another planet in terms of talent and efficiency.

Harrison will be significantly better on the Texans than he was over his last 10 games with the Cardinals, when he was the WR51 on WR40 usage. His -12% completion percentage over expected was 76th out of 87 qualifiers, largely due to his own issues but also partially because of QB play. Stroud is a way better version of Jacoby Brissett, and this role as the primary Z receiver in Houston will be way better for his own skillset than being the downfield X receiver in Arizona. There will be more shallow and intermediate breaking routes, bunched sets, at-snap motions, slot work and other ways to hide his speed-based limitations. Stroud also knows Harrison well from their time together at Ohio State, so this chemistry should be established quickly. 

While the per-target results should be better, Harrison must completely ice Hutchinson and Boutte for snaps to be an upside WR4 in fantasy. The Texans were rotating their WRs before this trade, and that simply can't happen. In the three games with Collins, target shares were Collins (26%), Hutchinson (17%), Boutte (11%) and Noel (10%). Hutchinson's expected half PPR points in that role equated to the WR51 per my model, so Harrison has to at least have the Hutchinson role to be relevant. That's not a high bar to clear, but the coaching staff can't continue to mix in the other boundary receivers at the expense of Harrison. For now, he is a quality bench stash who will be better in November and December than right away. He'd be in the Jordan Addison, Dontayvion Wicks and Romeo Doubs tier for my rest-of-season ranking as a WR4/5. That's way better than what he would've been rotting away in the desert. He was the worst sixth- or seventh-round pick in fantasy this year:

There is obviously no room for anyone else in the WR room. Noel should slide into 3-WR sets as the primary slot, while Hutchinson and Boutte become extremely small parts of the rotation as insurance or run-game options. Dalton Schultz will have more relevance than them, but Schultz is the TE18 on TE12 usage in games with Collins since 2025. Introducing another red-zone threat to the team should send him to very clear TE2 land.

Montgomery (groin) "may miss some time" per Ryans, so it should be more Marks than usual. This trade shouldn't really impact the running back position much. They might run a little less with this 3-WR set, but they will also move the ball better, giving the team more red-zone chances. It'll all even out. How Marks and Montgomery fare will largely be dependent on if one can separate from the other. To my eyes, it's not close. Marks is better. He's also healthier, younger and would fit this more spread style offense, if that's what is coming.

item.title: Detroit Lions expected to lose WR/RET Tom Kennedy to season-ending injury
item.description: The Detroit Lions will be on the hunt for a returner as Tom Kennedy’s season is reportedly likely over.
item.content:encoded:
Detroit Lions wide receiver/returner Tom Kennedy’s 2026 season is almost certainly over, as NFL Network’s Mike Garafolo reports that the Lions returner is expected to undergo surgery to repair an MCL injury suffered in Week 5:

“Tom Kennedy suffered a significant MCL injury that is expected to require surgery and will end his season […] Dan Campbell was hopeful Kennedy’s absence would be shorter but further testing revealed the extent of the damage.”

In the first half of the Lions game against the Arizona Cardinals, Kennedy returned a punt and was awkwardly tackled, pinning his right knee under the Cardinals player. He was originally listed as questionable to return, but after halftime, he was declared out, as the early test did not look great, according to Lions coach Dan Campbell.

“It doesn’t look good, as far as anything short-term,” Campbell said. “We’ll know a lot more tomorrow. I think it could be a sprain somewhere in there–a pretty good sprain.”

Those follow-up tests Monday morning led to the diagnosis Garafolo reported and the speculation that he won’t play again this season.

Kennedy was the Lions’ primary punt and kick returner, and there is no clear answer for who will replace him in those roles. Starting wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown took over emergency punt return duties, but the Lions won’t want to subject him to the extra punishment that comes with the role and will likely need a different option. On kick returns, cornerback Khalil Dorsey was the emergency option to line up opposite Jacob Saylors, and his speed and experience could keep him in play as a replacement. Dorsey does not have NFL experience as a punt returner, so he likely is not in the running for that position.

With the Lions headed into a bye week, and Kennedy’s injury being season-ending, they can take their time before placing him on injured reserve and finding a replacement. Stay tuned to Pride of Detroit for updates on this situation as it unfolds.

item.title: Chiefs sign wide receiver Justin Watson to practice squad
item.description: Kansas City is reuniting with a familiar face by bringing the wide receiver onto the practice squad.
item.content:encoded:
After the bye week, Kansas City Chiefs head coach Andy Reid met with local media via video call on Monday. Before taking any questions, he revealed the Chiefs are signing former wide receiver Justin Watson to the practice squad.

Reid explained why the team is bringing back Watson, who played in Kansas City from 2022-2024 before signing a free-agent contract with the Houston Texans in 2025. He played two games before suffering a calf/Achilles injury that landed him on the Reserve/Injured list until the season finale; he also appeared on special teams for Houston in the postseason.

“He was a good player for us when he was here,” Reid said. “Obviously, he can run, and he’s fast; he has great size. He’s willing to do everything; he knows the offense; he’s a smart kid.

To make room for the practice-squad signing, Reid explained that wide receiver Tyquan Thornton (dislocated ankle) will be placed on the Reserve/Injured list and linebacker Cam Jones will be signed to the active roster.

During his time with the Chiefs, Watson was a downfield option who seemed to impact the game almost exclusively by hauling in deep passes from quarterback Patrick Mahomes. In his brief stint with Houston, he caught only three passes over three games, but in Kansas City, he caught 64 passes over three years; 49 of them came on throws 10 or more yards downfield, according to Pro Football Focus.

“We felt like he could come back in and, as needed, contribute,” Reid said. “Step in and go with just a slight review, he should be fine and good to go.”

The 30-year-old Watson is listed at 6 feet 2 inches tall and 215 pounds, “great size,” as Reid put it. Before the Tampa Bay Buccaneers selected him in the fifth round of the 2018 NFL Draft, he ran the 40-yard dash in 4.42 seconds at the University of Penn Pro Day and recorded a vertical leap (40 inches) that would have tied for first among receivers at that year’s NFL Combine.

That was over eight years ago, but the team clearly sees value in bringing Watson back into the fold now that Thornton, the team’s primary downfield threat, will likely miss the remainder of the season.

“Tyquan was doing a tremendous job,” Reid said. “It was nice to see Xavier get a deep one in the game also; we know he can do all that. Then the other guys will mix in; they all have good speed and ability to get down the field as needed.”

Reid was asked directly about whether wide receiver Xavier Worthy’s role could change due to Thornton’s injury.

“Xavier actually had a strong game the other day,” Reid began. “He’s going to continue to be a target, for sure. I don’t know how much his role will change. He has a big part of the pass game to start with, so I’m sure that will continue on.”

When asked about rookie wideout Cyrus Allen’s spot in the rotation, Reid sounded open to the idea of seeing more from the training camp standout.

“I think he would probably work into the mix there a little bit more,” Reid shared. “He’s a good football player; even though he’s young, he has good ability.”

Kansas City should absolutely see what players like Allen and second-year wideout Jalen Royals can do with more playing time after the Thornton injury, but don’t be surprised if you see Watson — presumably No. 84 again — streaking downfield on a deep pass from Mahomes soon.

item.title: Arizona football: 5 things we learned from the 1st half of the 2026 season
item.description: Arizona has reached the halfway point in its season and heads into the bye week with a lot of confidence. The Wildcats (5-1, 2-1 Big 12) have not always played to perfection but more often than not they are getting the job done. Things won’t be getting easier for Arizona but the good news is […]
item.content:encoded:
Arizona has reached the halfway point in its season and heads into the bye week with a lot of confidence. The Wildcats (5-1, 2-1 Big 12) have not always played to perfection but more often than not they are getting the job done.

Things won’t be getting easier for Arizona but the good news is that four of the final six games are at Casino Del Sol Stadium. Right now, the UA is still in the hunt for a berth in the Big 12 Championship but only time will tell if it will find its way to Arlington in December.

Here are five things that we have learned through the first half of Arizona’s 2026 campaign:

So goes Fifita, so goes Arizona

Going into this season, Noah Fifita was the undisputed leader of the Wildcats. There was some optimism that some returners and maybe even some new faces could make Fifita’s job easier.

However, now due to some injuries and with the offensive line slowly coming along, the reliance on Fifita’s strong performances is very high. While Fifita has not always been perfect, his ability to respond to adversity has been the difference in many games.

It’s pretty clear that as long as the Wildcats are not turning the ball over, and Fifita is finishing drives in the end zone, the offense will get the job done. It also seems like the defense feeds off of what Fifita and the offense does.

Playing for one another is a standard across the program, but wanting to play for and not let down Fifita also seems to be extra motivation for the Wildcats. Everyone in the locker room wants to make the fifth year quarterback’s last season one for the record books.

Brent Brennan recognizes just how fortunate Arizona is to have Fifita at quarterback. He makes everyone’s lives easier and makes wins that much more meaningful.

“I’ll tell you guys every day, twice a day, if you want to hear it. I’m so glad Noah Fifita plays for Arizona,” said Brennan after the Cincinnati win.

Offensive line slowly figuring it out

It has not been all sunshine and rainbows for the offense, even with Fifita being the difference maker he is. There was a three game stretch where the offensive line allowed a sack on the first offensive play of the game.

Despite the first play setbacks, in the last two games Arizona has still been able to find the end zone on that first drive. The line also did not start the season off strong in getting the run game going.

In two of the first three games, the Wildcats were held to under 100 yards rushing. Since then, it has shown signs of improvement. In the last three games, Arizona has reached the 100 yard mark in every game, including a 238 yard performance against Cincinnati.

“I know our running game hasn’t been as explosive as it was early last year, but if you look at the way they’re running, they’re about as physical as I’ve ever seen,” said Seth Doege. ”So I’m not down on our running backs.”

The running backs have been physical in their runs all season, but now with the offensive line figuring it out, the explosiveness is starting to show. Arizona has had 17 plays that resulted in runs of 10+ yards in the last three games.

Where things started to turn was the fourth quarter in Pullman. The Wildcats were able to lean on the Cougars and wear them down to create strong running lanes and move the pile.

“I thought that we really started to move them in the second half, and I thought that was impactful because they were playing good defense,” said Brennan after the Washington State win. “It was great to see that momentum swing in the second half for us, and where that run game became really impactful.”

There are still things to clean up with blocking assignments and penalty issues, and that’s why the bye week comes at a perfect time. If Arizona can translate the run success into the second half of the season, then the offense as a whole will be a constant threat.

WRs are ready for the moment

Giovanni Richardson left the BYU game with an undisclosed injury, but was able to come back against Cincinnati. The injury seems to have come back as he did not finish that game, along with the other two Arizona starting wide receivers.

Tre Spivey is now out for the season with a foot injury, and Chris Hunter III is out for the foreseeable future with an undisclosed injury. With the injuries piling up, the players that have come in have not flinched.

Many wideouts have seized their opportunity, whether they are a veteran player or a young guy, they are finding a connection and building trust with Fifita. Starting with a guy who has waited his turn, junior Brandon Phelps made his mark from the get-go.

On the season, he has 12 receptions for 223 yards and three touchdowns. Behind him, sophomore Isaiah Mizell is coming off a breakout performance at West Virginia. He had six catches for 183 yards and two touchdowns. 

Mizell has 19 receptions for 359 yards and four touchdowns this season, but he’s not the only young gun showing out for the Wildcats. Caleb “Jet” Smith is now Arizona’s most dynamic receiver when he is in space.

Smith’s breakout performance came in the win at Washington State where he had four catches for 86 yards and a touchdown. He is also a very dangerous player on special teams as he has 125 punt return yards and a touchdown.

All have shown an ability to produce and have filled in well for the injured Wildcats. Whoever has the hot-hand is the receiver that Fifita will rely on but all are reliable and Fifita knows he can distribute the ball to everyone.

Defense gets it done by committee

One constant with Danny Gonzales’ defense is that every player runs to the ball. No jogging to the ball, no walking to the ball, no dancing to the ball (unless it’s fast). Gonzales wants as many bodies to the ball as possible.

Arizona has 13 defenders who have 10+ tackles on the season. A pair of linebackers lead the Wildcats in tackles with Taye Brown in first with 39 and Cooper Blomstrom in second with 30.

The Wildcats have 45 tackles for loss with Chase Kennedy leading the way with 5.5 tackles for loss. They also have 19 sacks on the season with Kennedy also leading that category with four on the season.

A reason for so many players being able to contribute is due to the heavy rotation that is used across the entire defense. The defensive front has a rotation, the secondary has a rotation, even the linebackers have one, although their rotation is shorter.

The rotation keeps bodies fresh and gives players a chance to make plays that perhaps wouldn’t be made without the rotation. While the drop off in turnovers from last season is not ideal, as long as the job is getting done then Arizona will stick to the rotation.

Run defense is Wildcats’ specialty

Outside of the game against West Virginia, the Wildcats’ run defense has improved since last season. In four out of the six games this season, Arizona has held its opponent to under 100 yards rushing. 

It held Cincinnati, the second best rushing attack in the Big 12 to just 74 total rushing yards. While West Virginia was able to run wild on the Wildcats, it made up for it with two fumble recoveries.

On the season, Arizona is holding its opponents to 3.3 yards per carry and just 116.3 yards per game. In the Big 12, the Wildcats are tied for seventh in rushing yards allowed. 

The standard is to hold every team to under 100 rushing yards, and given the way Gonzales runs his players in practice, it’s easy to see how successful Arizona is at group tackling.

“We go into every game wanting to hold people under 100 yards,” said Gonzales. “Demand excellence, demand a standard, and if we play aggressive and fast and physical, it makes it hard for them to do it.”

item.title: Chiefs bring WR Justin Watson back to their practice squad
item.description: Wide receiver Justin Watson is back with the Chiefs.
item.content:encoded:
Wide receiver Justin Watson is back with the Chiefs.

Head coach Andy Reid said at a Monday press conference that the Chiefs have signed Watson to their practice squad. Watson played for the Chiefs from 2022-2024 and moved on to the Texans last season, but he has been a free agent since being released at the end of August.

Watson had 64 catches for 1,064 yards and seven touchdowns in 50 regular season games for Kansas City. He also had nine catches for 120 yards during three postseasons with the team and he helped the Chiefs win a pair of Super Bowls.

The Chiefs saw wideout Tyquan Thornton go down with a dislocated ankle in Week 4 and there was some talk of interest in bringing Tyreek Hill back in the wake of that injury, but the Chiefs have opted for a different reunion as they come out of their bye week.
