The offense looked as good as it has all year with Kevin O’Connell giving game balls to Kyler Murray, Justin Jefferson, and Aaron Jones. Will Reichard […]
item.content:encoded:
The Minnesota Vikings have moved to 5-0 beating the New Orleans Saints, 23-13. The game wasn’t as close as the score was. The Vikings defense continues to dominate teams. The offense looked as good as it has all year with Kevin O’Connell giving game balls to Kyler Murray, Justin Jefferson, and Aaron Jones.

Will Reichard

The team’s MVP continued his perfect season, going 3-for-3 on field goals and 2-for-2 on extra points. Reichard has become much more than just a reliable kicker. He’s a legitimate weapon and a difference-maker. It feels like every time Minnesota crosses midfield, three points are almost automatic.

Kyler Murray

Murray wasn’t spectacular, but he did enough. With Addison and Darrisaw out and Hockenson going down early, the Vikings didn’t need him to play hero ball. They just needed him to avoid the killer mistake.

Aaron Jones

Jones did have a costly fumble in the red zone, but it shouldn’t overshadow another outstanding performance. Ever since Jordan Mason went down, Jones has carried a massive workload and continued to deliver. His 113 rushing yards helped control the tempo of the game and kept the Saints defense on the field. Hopefully there is help coming after the upcoming bye.

Byron Murphy Jr.

Murphy put together one of the best games of his Vikings career. He came away with two interceptions and essentially erased his side of the field, allowing just three yards in coverage. The pressure generated up front certainly helped, but Murphy took advantage of every opportunity that came his way. The Vikings defense continues to overwhelm opponents, and Murphy has developed into one of the biggest reasons why.

Brian Flores

The Vikings are 5-0 because of Brian Flores’ defense. Every week it’s difficult to single out just one player because everybody seems to be contributing. One week it’s Dallas Turner. The next week it’s Byron Murphy Jr. Then it’s Jalen Redmond, Blake Cashman, or Eric Wilson. Flores has built a defense where all 11 players are flying around and making plays. The Vikings have held opponents under 20 points in every game this season and continue to force turnovers at critical moments. At some point, the credit has to go to the guy putting everyone in position to succeed. Flores continues to dial up pressure, confuse quarterbacks, and make offenses look uncomfortable for four quarters. When it’s impossible to pick just one defensive player, it’s usually a good time to recognize the coach behind it all.

item.title: Raiders outclassed, out-performed by Patriots in humbling 45-17 loss
item.description: Las Vegas has no answers as all three phases of the game struggle mightily against New England in lopsided road defeat
item.content:encoded:
There was no escaping the quick sand on Sunday for the Las Vegas Raiders.

That same resolve and resilience the team produced to overcome adversity and surge to a 3-0 start to the 2026 campaign under head coach Klint Kubiak and his coaching staff, was non-existent in Foxborough as the Silver & Black were thoroughly throttled by the host New England Patriots 45-17.

The glaring absence of complementary football from the Raiders allowed the Patriots to outclass and out-perform the visitors and it was a contest where the offense, defense, and special teams was so out of whack, one had to openly wonder if Las Vegas got off the plane in New England.

The lopsided humbling defeat was the first time where Las Vegas coaching staff truly looked neophyte — Kubiak and his chosen defensive coordinator Rob Leonard are rookies in their respective roles — and the seasoned veterans of head coach Mike Vrabel and offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels took full advantage.

In total, McDaniels — a former Raiders head coach and play caller himself — dialed up an offense that dropped 536 total yards (371 through the air, 165 on the ground) on Leonard’s surprisingly soft defense. Kubiak’s offense couldn’t find that kind of success as Zak Kuhr’s Patriots defense stymied the Raiders to the tune of 306 total yards (268 passing and a meager 38 rushing).

The drubbing was so thorough that even sure-handed elite tight end Brock Bowers lost the ball on an impressive punch out by the Patriots defense — adding to the Raiders’ all-game misery.

What truly makes the defeat disheartening for the Raiders: The Patriots were decimated by injury heading into this contest missing key elements on offense, defense, and special teams but didn’t let that hinder them. They showcased determination, resolve, and sense of urgency — all of which Kubiak’s team exhibited to go 3-1 heading into this game.

Instead, McDaniels and the Patriots get a measure of revenge for the 20-13 2025 season-opening loss the team suffered at the hands of the Raiders in New England last season. Of course, we know how that went as the trajectory for both teams were polar opposites.

After Sunday’s result, the conversation goes from “What’s wrong with Drake Maye?” to “What’s wrong with Klint Kubiak and Rob Leonard?” — highlighting how quickly narratives in the NFL can change.

There’s plenty of teach tape for the Raiders, however. And once again, Kubiak did well to take ownership of the team’s issues and result against the Patriots. As I noted earlier this past week, accountability is great, but without action to correct the issues is troublesome. Fortunately for Kubiak and Co., they have several opportunities this season to show they are indeed all about that action. And the first is against the incoming Bills next Sunday at home.

Credit to New England for showcasing the ugly warts Las Vegas has. It was there for anyone to see. All eyes turn to the Raiders coaching staff and players ensuring that was an anomaly and not habit.

That said, we did get to see Las Vegas No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza get snaps at quarterback. Brief as it was, the experience was a good one for the Indiana product.

Let’s hit the quick slants as fast as the Patriots put peddle to the metal and boat raced the visiting Raiders:

—New England’s seven explosive plays (for 20 yards or more) against the Las Vegas defense was eye opening as McDaniels dialed up an aggressive attacking scheme, one that they deployed to stun the Buffalo Bills in Week 4. The Patriots opened the game with a 35-yard touchdown reception by DeMario Douglas and then got a 34-yard TD catch from Kyle Williams in the third quarter.

—In comparison, Las Vegas generated just three explosive plays — Bowers’ 28-yard catch, Ashton Jeanty’s 31-yard catch-and-run, and Cody White’s 28-yard grab. That 31-yard reception from Jeanty marked the team’s longest play while the 49-yard catch from Williams marked New England’s longest play of the day.

—Kubiak’s ground game continues to struggle with a pathetic 38 yards on 18 carries (2.1 yards per carry average) with the longest run being five-yard gains by Dylan Laube, Mike Washington Jr., and Tre Tucker. McDaniels’ run game, in comparison, was a group effort with Rhamondre Stevenson leading the group with 64 yards on 13 carries and Corey Kiner adding 52 yards on six totes.

—Turnover prone heading into the matchup, Maye didn’t lose the ball once while dropping dimes all over the field racking up four passing touchdowns and running another one in for five total end zone visits. May was comfortable in the pocket and surgically dissected the Raiders secondary going 26 of 34 for 374 yards and getting sacked just once.

—McDaniels offense found the end zone six times — four through the air and twice on the ground — having it’s way with Leonard’s defense that couldn’t pressure May. The result of Maye having seemingly all day to throw was throwing over Raiders defensive backs sprinting to recover. Other than Bowers’ first-quarter touchdown catch, Las Vegas struggled throughout with Laube’s two-yard plunge in the fourth quarter the only other TD.

—Cousins finished 19 of 28 for 243 yards and a touchdown. He didn’t throw an interception but was sacked three times and hit quite often. With the game out of hand, he ceded to rookie Fernando Mendoza and the No. 1 pick went six of eight for 48 yards with one carry for three yards.

—Bowers paced the Raiders air attack with 110 yards and a touchdown on eight receptions. The de facto WR1 continues to showcase he’s a tight end in name only as he was deployed all over the alignment, even in spots normally reserved for a traditional wide receiver. Jeanty added 50 yards on three catches while White had two grabs for 44 yards.

Quotes of Note

Up Next

The Bills are set to visit Allegiant Stadium next Sunday for an AFC afternoon clash in Las Vegas. Buffalo (3-1 overall) is looking to rebound from the Week 4 loss to New England and stay ahead in the AFC East race in their Monday Night matchup with the Los Angeles Rams (2-2). Interestingly enough, tonight’s clash features the two teams the Raiders play the next two weeks. First come the Bills, then a week later, the Rams roll into Allegiant.

item.title: Struggling Jake Ferguson keeps dropping the ball for the Cowboys
item.description: Cowboys fans are pretty upset with Jake Ferguson.
item.content:encoded:
Since stepping into the starting role in 2023, tight end Jake Ferguson has cemented himself as a key component of the Dallas Cowboys’ offense. His quick emergence allowed the team to transition away from Dalton Schultz to Ferguson at a much lower price. The young tight end quickly earned the trust of Dak Prescott, establishing himself as a reliable safety valve and a vibrant source of energy for the offense.

Through his first four years in the league, he put together two Pro Bowl seasons as he found ways to find soft spots in coverage and make the most of every reception with impressive toughness and the occasional hurdle of defenders. Having a seam-stretching tight end who commanded attention helped make a dynamic Cowboys offense even more dynamic. Fans loved him.

Last July, Ferguson signed a four-year, $52 million extension with the team, putting him under team control through the 2029 season. While his athleticism and locker room energy made him a guy the team wanted to hold on to, a pattern of costly mistakes is starting to raise questions about his overall consistency and long-term effectiveness.

In past seasons, the veteran tight end has shown good hands, making contested catches look effortless, but recently his focus has wavered at critical moments. Through five games this year, he has a drop rate of 9.5%, which is a high percentage for a player targeted on short-to-intermediate routes. Obviously, the most devastating example came on Thursday night when the ball was thrown right at his grill. Not only did he not secure the catch, but the ball deflected off his face and stayed in the air forever until a Buccaneers defender could safely get under it. A potential comeback drive turned into a costly game-ending mistake.

Even more alarming than the periodic drop is Ferguson’s ongoing battle with ball security after the catch. Over the last three years, he’s put the ball on the turf a staggering eight times, leading all tight ends in that span. That’s a rate of once every 19.6 times he touches the ball. For perspective, that is like a running back who touches the ball 20 times a game who fumbles once every game. That’s atrocious.

His fumbling woes have caused opposing defensive coordinators to openly admit to going after him. Ferguson has a bad habit of carrying the ball away from his frame, making him vulnerable to aggressive defenders who deliberately swipe at the ball. And it’s worked. He had a costly fumble on a shovel pass against the Baltimore Ravens a couple of weeks ago that erased a promising scoring drive. We can argue until we are blue in the face about whether that should’ve been ruled incomplete, but either way, Ferguson isn’t doing a good job securing the ball.

These things are harmful to the team, but some might be willing to give him a little leniency if he were a strong blocker. He’s not. His chip blocks are ineffective, and he routinely misses his blocking assignments in the running game. There are more and more instances of Ferguson being tossed aside as a blocker. It’s not good.

The Cowboys invested a second-round pick in Luke Schoonmaker in 2023, but he has not worked out as planned. The team reupped on Ferguson, but now, suddenly, he has created a bit of concern as well. The front office also wisely extended Brevyn Spann-Ford, who is the team’s gritty blocker and special teams contributor, but one can’t help wondering if we could see a change in responsibilities as the season moves forward. If Ferguson can’t clean up some of his problems and start being more of a net positive than a liability, the Cowboys might have some tough decisions ahead.

item.title: David Montgomery, Jalen Pitre considered week-to-week
item.description: The Texans have a couple of injury concerns coming out of Sunday’s win over the Titans.
item.content:encoded:
The Texans have a couple of injury concerns coming out of Sunday’s win over the Titans.

Head coach DeMeco Ryans told reporters on Monday that both running back David Montgomery (groin) and safety Jalen Pitre (shoulder) are considered week-to-week.

Montgomery has started each of the first five games for Houston this season, rushing for 138 yards on 52 carries with a pair of touchdowns. Second-year back Woody Marks leads the team with 149 yards on 43 carries with two TDs.

Pitre has also started all five games for Houston this season, registering five passes defensed, a fumble recovery and 24 total tackles.

The Texans will be headed across the pond to play the division rival Jaguars in London on Sunday.

item.title: Dan Quinn remains employed for now, somehow
item.description: Most coaches in the NFL either have been fired or will be fired.
item.content:encoded:
Most coaches in the NFL either have been fired or will be fired. Dan Quinn has been fired (by the Falcons) and he undoubtedly will be fired again (by the Commanders).

For now, the Commanders haven't fired him.

Some have suggested that Sunday's colossal blunder seals Quinn's fate at the end of the year. Properly functioning organizations, however, will implement the decision as soon as it's made, if only to begin the process of searching for the next coach. Really, what's the point of prolonging the situation?

In this case specifically, any effort by Quinn to turn a 1-3-1 season into a playoff berth will be complicated by the task of getting the locker room to do anything other than roll their eyes when the time comes to listen to Quinn. The sooner the organization turns the page on the person responsible for the worst ending to a game since the Joe Pisarcik moment in 1978, the sooner the team can move on.

There's a dotted line back to Super Bowl XLIX, Quinn's last game with the Seahawks. While he wasn't there for the aftermath of the fateful decision to throw the ball at the goal line, Pete Carroll dealt with the fumes of costing the Legion of Boom its "dynasty" label for years. Quinn, who has only weeks to work with, will have a very hard time burying this one.

The issue won't go away quickly. It will be the topic of the week in D.C. Quinn will be asked about it again. Quarterback Jayden Daniels will be asked about it again. Offensive coordinator David Blough — who has yet to receive nearly as much blame as he should — will be asked about it. Other players will be asked about it.

Come next Monday, when the Commanders play the 49ers in Santa Clara, it will be a focal point of the ESPN pregame show. It will be mentioned once or twice (or more often) throughout the call of the game.

Can Quinn turn it around? The 2017 Falcons made it to the playoffs, after the 28-3 debacle in Super Bowl LI. But Quinn and the Falcons had an entire offseason with which to process their meltdown. For the Commanders, the next train is already on the tracks.

The bye is looming after next Monday night. Could ownership decide to give Quinn a chance to right the ship in San Francisco? Could an embarrassment next week be the final straw?

The problem is that the ultimate embarrassment has already unfolded. While stranger things have happened, it's hard to imagine Quinn and the Commanders quickly putting this behind them. The process can't even begin until Quinn finds a way to pull the locker room together again.

How can he do that? The players will be grumbling about this one deep into the coming workweek. Or possibly all the way through Monday and into the week off. What can he say to them to get them to understand how and why it happened?

He can continue to take the blame, but there's no honor in acknowledging the obvious. He'll need to find a way to get them to accept the fact that he made a mistake that never should have been made, and to persuade them to believe that the team is in good hands, notwithstanding Sunday's events.

Maybe an "us against the world" approach will emerge. The problem is that, in this case, the world is right. And the only way to make things right in Washington's world will be for the team to deliver the clearest, strongest message of accountability by relieving the person responsible for the situation of his duties.

item.title: Giants-Commanders: 5 plays that led to this game ending in a tie
item.description: Five plays that define this 27-27 tie.
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants tied the Washington Commanders in an epic comeback on Sunday, with emotional swings that could fracture one’s spirit. New York battled back from a 27-13 deficit in the final eight minutes. Jameis Winston finished with 326 passing yards and three touchdowns. The game had frustrating moments and very impressive individual efforts, but missed field goals and a costly Cam Skattebo fumble took the win away from the Giants. However, Washington was in position to win this game multiple times, but destiny dictated that neither team would win this football game. Here are five plays or sequences of plays that defined this wacky game.

Play(s) 1: The Giants don’t go away

The Giants are a resilient team. They were frustrating for most of the game. They were inefficient on the ground, made terrible defensive lapses, and the Jameis Winston Experience was on full display. Despite all of this, the Giants tied the game in the fourth quarter — the Giants just didn’t go away!

Winston put the team ON HIS BACK and led three consecutive touchdown drives that totaled 32 plays, and resulted in two Isaiah Likely touchdowns and a Malik Nabers touchdown. It felt bleak, but the Giants battled back to send the game to overtime – that’s impressive resilience and excellent coaching. The Giants play with pride.

Play(s) 2: What?!

The Giants led an improbable comeback where they were down 27-13 to start the fourth quarter. The defense forced a punt after one of Dominic Zvada’s sthree missed field goals and the Giants ripped off 67 yards on eight plays, where it looked like they were going to win the game, but Skattebo fumbled. Washington drove the football down the field and got into field goal range, but with not timeouts…this happened!

Dan Quinn took responsibility by saying this, but questioning Jayden Daniels’ actions only makes sense.

Play 3: Slow start to on defense again, SPY THE GUY

No defense wants to go down seven in the first three plays of the game, but Dennard Wilson’s unit found themselves in that exact situation. PISTOL power run with presnap motion from the H-Back and Josh Conerly (72) pulling to the play side. Washington beat the Giants to the fit and Tyler Nubin (27) took another bad angle that his athletic ability could not rectify – an unfortunate all too familiar sight. The result was this 33-yard touchdown run by Jacory Croskey-Merritt. 

It’s not all on Nubin; he’s the face that will rightfully be chastised, but several Giants failed to execute their assignments well, which placed Nubin in that position. C.J. Okoye (99) is removed from the gap and Arvell Reese (52) was picked up by Conerly. Tremaine Edmunds (49) was washed to the inside by the climbing offensive lineman, and the seas were parted by Washington. 

Also, the Giants ran a lot of man coverage last week in their win over Arizona. It was successful, but Jayden Daniels has a bit more mobility than Jacoby Brissett. The Giants were burnt TWICE on Daniels’ rushing touchdowns against man coverage. 

I’m not sure if it’s a blown assignment by the Giants or just questionable play calling – either way, it has to be fixed.

Play 4: Jameis’ fumble

The Giants tried to run an under center play action shot on second-and-8. Winston looked to Malik Nabers’ quick curl, which was promptly covered by Jeremey Reeves (39). Bryan Hudson (60) was backed into the pocket slowly by Tim Settle (97) and Deatrich Wise Jr. (91) hit Winston, as the veteran quarterback attempted to fall on the football. Tim Settle of Washington recovered, giving Daniels excellent field position, which resulted in a 40 yard field goal. 

Great job by the Giants defense to stiffen and force only a field goal. Up until this point of the game, the Giants’ offense showed very little. They had 41 total yards, which would obviously change.

Play(s) 5: Controversy 

The Giants scored after a 13-play, 63 yard drive that took up seven minutes of game clock. However, the drive was seemingly stopped by an Amik Robertson interception on the goal line:

The interception was negated by a defensive pass interference against Robertson. Is there contact? Yes. Is it egregious? No. It’s not the worst call in the world – we see the tug – but I’ve seen much worse not called, and it was a risky – bad – throw by Winston. The call gave the Giants the football back and Likely finished the job with the touchdown below: 

The Giants stretched the zone defense toward the sideline with the the routes of Malachi Fields (88) and Darnell Mooney (17); Likely, then, slipped into the vacated spot and Winston just got the football toward his inside shoulder for six. The Giants reduced the lead to six points heading into the fourth quarter.

Another somewhat controversial play happened to give the Giants’ life in the fourth quarter on fourth down. Isaiah Likely’s second touchdown:

It does seem like Likely broke the plane of the goal line, though. Both of these plays were obviously consequential in the comeback.

EXTRA

Play(s) 6: The J.J. McCarthy Package

The Giants had plays designed with McCarthy as the quarterback – none of them worked. The first was a blown up touch-pass to Darnell Mooney that was easily sniffed out by Washington. The second was a solid screen pass to Malik Nabers that was called back by an illegal formation. Then, on third-and-2, Matt Nagy tried to leverage McCarthy’s athletic ability and ran a jet-zone-read that Frankie Luvu easily sensed and blew up, which led to a Dominic Zvada 56-yard field goal. McCarthy also ran a zone-read that gained 1 yard.

It’s obvious the Giants want to use McCarthy’s mobility, but it did not work in Washington, as Nagy tried to do anything to get the offense going.

item.title: Sunday Aftermath: Jeremiyah Love's struggles, the Packers' outburst, and more
item.description: Breaking down all of the NFL's biggest Week 5 storylines, including Jeremiyah Love's ongoing struggles.
item.content:encoded:
On the day they traded Marvin Harrison Jr., the Cardinals probably couldn’t help but wonder if Jeremiyah Love will be next. Not next month or even next year, but some inevitable time down the line. It’s been that kind of decade for the Birds, who never really got up to highway speeds with Kyler Murray, and remained stuck in neutral with Harrison. Rather consciously or not, Love seems to have internalized that this is a place that wastes its young talent, and it seems to have made him miserable.

For their part, the Cardinals seem determined to prove him right. Love’s most unassailable usage came in their second game — of the preseason. That’s where he picked up an ankle injury still bothering him to this day. Love was fit to be unleashed on August 13 against the Raiders but apparently not on September 13 against the Chargers. He had fewer touches in the Cardinals’ season opener (13) than he did against the Silver and Black (14).

That’s a number he’s risen above just twice in five regular season appearances. If you draft a running back at No. 3 overall, it is presumably to do everything. You can’t take an RB in the top five if they are going to be part of a committee. But the Cardinals seem to barely trust Love to do anything. Tyler bleeping Allgeier, who caught 61 passes during the entirety of his rookie contract, is the Cards’ third down and two-minute drill back. “Make it make sense,” you say, but you know you can’t.

Now nursing long-term injuries to both ankles in addition to his ego, Love seems unlikely to “get right” any time soon. Fantasy managers just have to pray it is before he meets the seemingly irrestible fate of all top-five Cardinals skill players: A ticket out of Arizona.

Five Week 5 Storylines

Jordan Love and the Packers finally play the offense they promised in the offseason. Laid low by their postseason devastation at the hands of the Bears, the Packers pledged to remake their system. They wanted to get the ball in their best players’ hands more often, and they wanted to better “finish” contests. Aka not take their foot off the gas and treat the second half as if the goal were to get the clock to zero rather than score the most points. The project had not been going too well through the first four weeks of the season. It turns out all they needed to get it right was the Bears themselves — and their backup quarterback. Yes, this was not the same Chicago team Green Bay will face later this year and perhaps again in the playoffs. But it was a demon that needed to be slayed, and it was done in spectacular fashion. If you watched the game, it felt like Love was completing a deep pass every other play. That’s because he was. Love’s 252 “completed air yards” were the most of his career. The Pack have been wanting to air out. They have finally done so. Hopefully it’s a taste of what’s to come instead of the precursor to another one of coach Matt LaFleur’s patented retreats.

Bears look human without Caleb Williams and Kyle Monangai. Which brings us to Chicago. Arguably no team had been flying higher despite the absence of its franchise player and starting quarterback. They had defeated teams with both their No. 2 and No. 3 quarterbacks. It seemed Ben Johnson could do no wrong. Maybe he can’t, but he was finally wronged by Tyson Bagent. There can only be so much smoke and so many mirrors. Sunday the smoke evaporated, the mirrors were smashed, and the Bears were vividly reminded of Williams’ importance, even if he doesn’t implement Johnson’s offense with the same precision as his automaton backups. Williams is a blunt-force instrument that both Johnson and fantasy managers desperately need. It appears we will finally get him in Week 6 against the Falcons.  

Snakebitten TreVeyon Henderson re-injures ankle. First off, it’s never a good thing when the word “latest” appears before the phrase “ankle injury.” That’s what Henderson is dealing with. Slated for a Monday MRI, missed time appears all but guaranteed. It, obviously, is the last thing Henderson or fantasy managers needed after a slow start to the 2026 season where Henderson failed to take advantage of Rhamondre Stevenson’s ongoing miscues. As unwanted as a potential injured reserve placement might be, it could buy players time as they assess their next move with a runner who seemed unlikely to force his way back into the RB2 ranks any time soon. If Henderson goes week to week, things get tougher with byes beginning in earnest and injuries mounting. In the meantime, “Corey Kiner” is now the next man up for the Pats.

Things get worse for the Eagles; It’s unclear how they’ll get better. The good news: The Eagles converted a third down. They even scored a few second half points. Emphasis on “a few” since it was only three, but yeah. Miraculously, they were somehow in position to win until one of the worst special teams mistakes in recent memory. That was the only near miracle in a game where Will Shipley joined Saquon Barkley, DeVonta Smith and Tank Bigsby on the shelf. Now the Eagles’ already-depleted depth is in the “Dameon Pierce zone,” with the even more ominous “Jaydon Blue zone” lurking. There’s no true “fix” here, and will be no hope of any kind until Barkley and Smith return. Until then, Jalen Hurts can no longer be treated as a QB1.

Justin Herbert goes from benchable to droppable. The only thing the Eagles really have going for themselves right now is that they’re not the Chargers. The sheer scale of the disaster is beyond Herbert’s control, but it’s a simple fact that even in the very worst setups, if you are a good quarterback, you won’t typically have five total touchdowns compared to nine total turnovers. We already stopped starting Herbert several weeks ago. Now it would appear the only appropriate course of action is dropping him. He also belongs outside the top 24 in superflex leagues until something changes. With basically everyone else hurt, it’s unclear what that fabled “change” might be.

Don't forget, for the latest on everything NFL, check out Rotoworld’s Player News, or follow @Rotoworld_FB or @RotoPat on Twitter/Bluesky.

Five More 5 Storylines

Marvin Harrison Jr. shipped to the Texans amidst the Sunday afternoon action. In the scope of the wider football world, a former top-five overall pick was just traded in part for a second-rounder. Better compensation than most were expecting, but a disastrous outcome for the Cardinals two years after they spent the No. 4 overall selection. Either way, a fascinating story. By our narrower fantasy football purview, however, the takeaway is … new Kayshon Boutte just dropped? Because whatever the Texans’ project for “MHJ” is, it’s going to be long term. For now, they just need someone else to clear space opposite Nico Collins, and to hopefully credibly fill in whenever Collins suffers his next soft-tissue injury. C.J. Stroud is playing much better than anyone who watched the 2025-26 postseason could have expected, but Harrison’s fantasy fortunes probably don’t rise above those of a volatile WR4 for the time being.

Slumping David Montgomery lost to injury vs. Titans. Harrison arrives in Houston as “D-Mont” checks out for a bit. Already amongst the league’s worst running backs this season, the last thing Montgomery needed was an injury. It compounds the problem for fantasy managers, who were facing uncomfortable questions about Montgomery’s place in their starting lineup. We should now at least get short-term clarity. D-Mont will be affixed to Week 6 benches, and perhaps beyond. If Woody Marks fares well in his absence, he will likely take over 1A duties. If he doesn’t, Montgomery comes back hopefully healthier and refreshed, perhaps as soon as Week 9 following the Texans’ Week 8 bye. Hold on if you can, but be prepared to let go if Marks hits the ground running.  

Broncos show very little following change at play-caller. About the only noticeable difference following Sean Payton’s inevitable play-calling coup was the collapse of RJ Harvey’s receiving work. Beyond that, it was more of the awful same. Barely-there QB2 returns for Bo Nix, and a complete inability for Jaylen Waddle to post WR2 numbers. Waddle has now finished below 40 yards receiving in 4-of-5 games as a Bronco, and below 20 in 3-of-5. I have tried to keep the WR2 faith, but how long can you keep ranking a player like that in the top 24? The answer is “no longer,” at least for Thursday’s short-week date with the Seahawks’ dominant pass D.

Deebo Samuel goes down for Niners offense running low on players. The 49ers actually got the best of that dominant Seattle pass defense, but they did so with another low-key performance from their nominal No. 2 receiver. Samuel went down like a ton of bricks on a third quarter rushing fumble, to the point onlookers were worried he had suffered a severe head injury. Instead it was a severe hamstring pull, the kind of issue that has frequently been Samuel’s Niners and fantasy downfall. Already struggling to produce despite a golden setup, Samuel could end up a drop if you can’t stash him on an I.R. spot. The returns have just not been strong enough, and Samuel’s injury recoveries have a way of lingering.

Jaylen Warren continues to look like the best player on the Steelers. The question is: Will it matter with Rico Dowdle (toe) close to return? It seems like the answer should be a no-brainer “yes” but when you spend the first four seasons of your career in a committee, you quickly become a typecast player. Even if you provide gangbusters returns on bell-cow usage like Warren has done the past three weeks, coaching staffs tend to psych themselves out with the “so and so has never handled these kinds of workloads before” line of thinking. It’s certainly true Warren has never handled these kinds of workloads. Each of the three highest snap percentages of his career have come in the past three weeks. But he’s held up remarkably well under the pounding. Any player is more likely to get hurt if they are on the field more. Hopefully the Steelers don’t mistake that league-wide generality for a Warren specific.  

Questions

1. How does the NFC East go winless in a week where two of its teams were playing each other?

2. Justin Herbert and Tua Tagovailoa are imploding at the same time. Did a star die or a moon explode somewhere?

3. Remember when Deshaun Watson was “back”?

Early Waivers Look (Players rostered in less than 50 percent of Yahoo leagues)

QB: Kirk Cousins (vs. BUF), Aaron Rodgers (@TB), Michael Penix Jr. (vs. CHI), Jameis Winston (vs. NO), Jalon Daniels (vs. PIT)
RB: Keaton Mitchell, Kendre Miller, Dameon Pierce, Samaje Perine, Kimani Vidal, Raheim Sanders, Corey Kiner
WR: Malik Washington, Keon Coleman, Keenan Allen, Tre Tucker, Adonai Mitchell, Kendrick Bourne, Derius Cooper
TE: Brenton Strange, Chig Okonkwo, Darren Waller, Pat Freiermuth, Tyler Higbee
DEF: 49ers (vs. WAS), Giants (vs. NO), Colts (vs. TEN), Panthers (@PHI)

Stats of the Week

Braelon Allen's 116 yards rushing against the Browns were nearly double his previous career high of 59. We finally got proof of plug-and-play RB2 concept.

Titans pain stat of the week via Buck Reising: “Robert Saleh’s 0-5 start with the Titans is worse than both of Brian Callahan’s first two seasons. 1-3 in 2024, 1-4 in 2025.”

185. That’s how many pass attempts C.J. Stroud has gone without an interception to begin the season. Rattle that stat off to someone who just woke up from a coma they went into following the Texans’ Divisional Round loss.

Awards Section 

Week 5 Fantasy All-Pro Team: QB Drake Maye, RB Jahmyr Gibbs, RB Jaylen Warren, WR Christian Watson, WR Parker Washington, WR Malik Nabers, TE Isaiah Likely

Week 5 All Bank Examiner Squad: QB Justin Herbert, RB Omarion Hampton, RB Jeremiyah Love, WR CeeDee Lamb, WR Jaylen Waddle, WR Carnell Tate, TE Mark Andrews

The Very Worst Play In The History Of The Sport Award: The Commanders’ walk-off clock 0:00ing.

How Does It Rain Exactly 2.7 Inches Every Game Award: MetLife Stadium.

The Please God Anything But That Andddddd You Did It Award: Tua Tagovailoa.

item.title: Fantasy Football: Malik Nabers back to being a target hog, plus more key stats that may go overlooked from Week 5
item.description: Joel Smyth takes you through 8 key stats to note for fantasy football coming out of Week 5.
item.content:encoded:
In fantasy football, you have to look back to move forward. Fantasy points are the goal, but how a player gets there is the key. Analyst Joel Smyth breaks down 8 numbers to know from Week 5 in order to win your matchup in Week 6 and beyond.

31.8%

Targets per route for Mike Evans this season, second among wide receivers to Jaxon Smith-Njigba. With six wideouts now injured in San Francisco, it’s up to Evans (and I guess Brandin Cooks?) to carry the load for the 49ers. When healthy, Evans has been everything the 49ers were looking for. He has five red-zone receptions (third among WR) and seven explosive plays (fourth among WR). He is somewhat limited in routes as a whole, but when he’s on the field, he’s the clear No. 1 WR in a top offense. Brock Purdy playing extremely well this season is a cherry on top. ​

20

Targets for Malik Nabers versus Washington. Jameis Winston has been a gem for fantasy receivers in the past, and has been the last two weeks for Nabers. It was against the Commanders secondary, and on a week-high 84 offensive plays, but 20 targets is 20 targets. After the first game and a half together, Nabers has become the clear focus for Winston and the offense, with a 39% first-read target share the last two weeks. Winston has thrown to his first read 75% of the time this season, the third-highest rate in the NFL, making the volume more consistent and trustworthy going forward. The same could be said for TE Isaiah Likely, who has a 31% first-read target share since Week 2. The Giants will match up against the Saints next week before a tougher part of the schedule.

83%

Snaps for Rhamondre Stevenson after TreVeyon Henderson went down with an ankle injury. Bell-cow Stevenson returned Sunday when his team needed him, posting his second straight 15+ fantasy point day. More importantly, the Patriots offense seems to be back. As a red-zone back, Stevenson’s value truly comes out when Drake Maye is playing like himself. Henderson’s injury could not only lead to his absence, but a slow return while giving Stevenson the opportunity to show he should still be the 1A of the offense. The schedule is looking real nice as well, with the following games leading up to the bye: Jets, Bears, Dolphins, Packers and Lions.

-1

Yards before contact for Bhayshul Tuten Sunday morning. The role continues to grow, amassing 22 of the 24 Jaguars’ RB carries, including the early-down passing role. The matchup in the trenches proved to be too much. Jacksonville had three plays from the one-yard line and couldn’t capitalize, were destroyed up front by Jalen Carter specifically and Tuten had to grind out 73 rushing yards after contact to reach double-digit fantasy points. As part of a top-10 scoring offense, if Tuten continues to control the Jaguars backfield, he’ll put together some monster games against easier matchups. Next week, however, is against the Texans, right before a Week 7 bye, frustrating luck for a player playing so well.  

Over the last 2 weeks ...

Bhayshul Tuten: 39 carries, 5 targets
All other Jags RBs: 8 carries, 3 targets https://t.co/FItZiMvYAy

— Jared Smola (@SmolaDS) October 12, 2026

0/5

Games in which Christian McCaffrey has 20+ touches this season. It’s not the end of the world, but it is a managing expectations alert. McCaffrey had 20+ touches in 13 of his 16 games last season, finishing the year with the top fantasy RB volume by a mile. This season, he’s been a little more in “LeBron James load management” mode. Kaelon Black gets a portion of the red-zone work and CMC’s receiving has been below average compared to his past seasons. The positive now. The goal line is his; even when Black’s got the ball down there, here comes McCaffrey to punch it in. He’s had all eight goal-line carries to begin the year. Second, although targets are down, there’s a good shot a big target day is coming, as Black has only two targets to McCaffrey’s 25. It may not be fantasy perfection, but McCaffrey should still finish as a top-10 RB with great week-to-week consistency.

1

Red-zone targets this season for DK Metcalf. Aaron Rodgers has thrown 18 of them, two for touchdowns to Pat Freiermuth on Sunday. Will it change? Somewhat. Last season Metcalf was second in red-zone targets to Kenny Gainwell, with three tight ends very close behind. Pittsburgh throws at the goal line a lot, but with Rodgers it has consistently been to running backs and tight ends, as they’ve accounted for 62% of targets in the red zone since 2025. Metcalf still had 13 red-zone targets last year, but without consistency in between the 20s, the lack of touchdowns has become more of a problem.  

13%

Target share for Harold Fannin Jr. on Sunday, a season low. As a rookie breakout in 2025, Fannin ended his season with an impressive 10 consecutive games with a 20% target share or higher. Through five games this season, he’s only hit that mark in two of them. Even with a surprisingly competent offense, Fannin hasn’t been able to get consistent production with Deshaun Watson at QB. He’s been a checkdown option at best, with zero designed targets on the season and only three red-zone targets. However, all three of those targets have gone for scores, and Fannin’s yards after catch ability has been just as good. The issue isn’t talent, rather his role. He’s far from the focal point and should be treated as such until something changes.

5

Touches for Alvin Kamara in Week 5. After a two-TD game following the injury of Travis Etienne Jr., Kamara fell down to Earth even harder than the Saints offense. Tyler Shough didn’t fare well against the Vikings defense, but Kamara’s role was the bigger issue. Kendre Miller controlled the ground attack, handling all four red-zone carries, and CJ Donaldson out-snapped Kamara 18 to 12. Even when in on passing downs, Kamara was forced to stay in to block against Minnesota's blitz. He’ll have more targets in the future, but I don’t think it’ll be enough to warrant a starting spot.

item.title: NFL Injury Report, Week 6: Latest news, updates, fantasy football analysis for Lamar Jackson, Caleb Williams, more players
item.description: We go over the latest injury news and updates heading into Week 6, providing a list of players fantasy football managers will need to track.
item.content:encoded:
Week 6 of the 2026 NFL season is on the horizon and we're heading into our first big bye week slate. Four teams — the Bengals, Lions, Vikings and Dolphins — won't be playing, which will leave some holes in your lineup, on top of an ever-growing injury report. Below we'll provide the latest news, updates and fantasy football analysis for the Week 6 NFL injury report.

Quarterback

  • Lamar Jackson, BAL (ankle)

  • Caleb Williams, CHI (hamstring)

  • Michael Penix Jr., ATL (ribs)

  • Baker Mayfield, TB (thumb)

Jackson: The Ravens held Jackson out for their Week 5 win on SNF against the Falcons. Baltimore is hopeful Jackson can return for Week 6 in a key spot against the rival Browns. Tyler Huntley was capable in the comeback victory over Atlanta, finishing with 201 yards and two touchdowns, plus 20 rushing yards and a score on the ground. If Jackson sits, Huntley is a decent streaming option in fantasy, particularly with Jared Goff and Joe Burrow on bye.

Williams: The Bears could have Williams back under center in Week 6, per NFL Network's Ian Rapoport. Williams has missed the past three games with a hamstring strain and Chicago has gone 2-1 with Case Keenum and Tyson Bagent splitting time. Things got a bit ugly in Week 5 in a 31-7 loss to Green Bay. Bagent threw two INTs and just 87 yards before being benched for Keenum, who also threw a pick. If Williams can get back into the lineup, he's good to fire up in fantasy, and should be a boost to all Bears receivers against the Falcons in Week 6.

Penix: The Falcons lost Penix late in their OT loss to Baltimore on SNF in Week 5. Tua Tagovailoa came in relief and, well, did Tua things, throwing a game-ending interception in OT. If Penix misses games again, it could sink Atlanta's passing game if Tagovailoa is forced to start. Bijan Robinson would mostly be fine for fantasy as a clear elite RB1 but his ceiling may come down. Drake London takes the biggest hit if Penix is out.

Running Back

  • Saquon Barkley, PHI (hamstring)

  • Quinshon Judkins, CLE (foot)

  • Kyle Monangai, CHI (toe)

  • David Montgomery, HOU (groin)

  • Breece Hall, NYJ (quad)

  • TreVeyon Henderson, NE (ankle)

  • Rico Dowdle, PIT (toe)

  • Will Shipley, PHI (foot)

Eagles RBs: Barkley missed Week 5's brutal loss in London to the Jaguars. Shipley was injured during the game, paving the way for Dameon Pierce to lead the backfield. He mustered only 14 yards on 11 carries. If the Eagles can get Barkley back for Week 6 against the Panthers, great. But there's an issue of depth and the offensive line just lost Lane Johnson to retirement. If Barkley returns, managers can play him but know that his upside is severely lacking. Pierce is worth a waiver wire claim in deeper formats with Shipley facing a potential multi-week absence, but would be a risky flex option if Barkley sits again. Also be on the lookout for Philly to add a back via trade or the free agent pool.

Montgomery: The Texans' lead back was injured in Week 5's win over Tennessee and did not return. Head coach DeMeco Ryans told reporters that Monty "may miss some time" due to the groin issue. If Montgomery is sidelined, Woody Marks would take over as the RB1 for Houston and see the bulk of the touches in Week 6 against the Jaguars in London. Dare Ogunbowale would see some snaps as the backup. Marks would be a good RB3/flex option with RB2 upside. Week 6 is a tough draw against Jacksonville, but the Giants and Chargers are solid gets for Marks if Montgomery's injury lingers.

Henderson: It's been a rough start to his second NFL season for Henderson, who left early with an ankle injury in Week 5's blowout win over Las Vegas. Corey Kiner got some snaps with Henderson out but it was mostly Rhamondre Stevenson getting the work. That had been the case, Stevenson leading the way with Henderson as the change-of-pace back. If Henderson is out, Stevenson is an even safer RB2 option, especially the way the Patriots have rebounded the past two weeks. New England's schedule sets up well moving forward, making Stevenson an appealing trade target.

Wide Receiver

  • CeeDee Lamb, DAL (quad)

  • DeVonta Smith, PHI (hamstring)

  • DJ Moore, BUF (shoulder)

  • Rashee Rice, KC (hamstring)

  • Jalen Coker, CAR (quad)

  • Roman Wilson, PIT (finger) — Expected to miss a few weeks

Lamb: This injury isn't believed to be serious, plus it happened on TNF against the Bucs in Week 5. That gives Lamb some extra time to rest before Week 6 against the Packers. Green Bay has been good against the pass this season, but haven't faced a QB of Dak Prescott's stature. If Lamb is healthy, you're obviously firing him up in all formats. If Lamb has to miss this game, George Pickens gets a boost while it could open things up for TE Jake Ferguson and WR Ryan Flournoy.

Tight End

item.title: Denver Broncos Stock Up, Stock Down: Week 5 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers
item.description: Well, it wasn’t pretty, but the Broncos perfected winning ugly last season, and they are continuing that this season with a 23-17 comeback victory over their divisional rivals, the Los Angeles Chargers. The struggles on offense continued throughout this one, but they did show some life late while the Broncos’ defense dominated for the most […]
item.content:encoded:
Well, it wasn’t pretty, but the Broncos perfected winning ugly last season, and they are continuing that this season with a 23-17 comeback victory over their divisional rivals, the Los Angeles Chargers. The struggles on offense continued throughout this one, but they did show some life late while the Broncos’ defense dominated for the most part, outside of a handful of rather bad plays. It wasn’t a perfect game by the Broncos by any means, but at the end of the day, they got the win and improved to 3-2 on the year.

Still, there are some things the Broncos need to improve on, and improve on quickly, if they want to continue having success this season.

Stock up and stock down is a weekly series where I go through the Denver Broncos’ 53-man roster and tell you which Broncos players’ stock is going up, down, or remains unchanged. After an ugly win vs. the Chargers on Sunday, we have a good mix of stock-ups and stock-downs today.

Quarterback

Bo Nix – Stock down: His early-season struggles continued on Sunday. He looked unconfident, lost, and simply did not play well. We have seen Nix go through stretches like this, but he eventually bounces back and improves as the season goes on. Still, this might be one of his worst stretches. I have faith that he will bounce back, because we have seen Nix play MUCH better than this, but it did not look good on Sunday vs. a banged-up 0-4 Chargers team.

Next up, a difficult Seattle Seahawks defense on a short week.

Jarrett Stidham – Unchanged: Veteran backup quarterback.

Sam Ehlinger – Unchanged: Emergency third-string quarterback.

Running Back

JK Dobbins – Stock up slightly: I am going slightly because, for most of this game, he was not very good. Lacked explosiveness and, at most, was getting three yards and a cloud of dust. He had just 27 yards through 3 quarters on Sunday, but had 41 yards on 6 carries in the 4th quarter when the Broncos went on a 13-0 run.

That fourth quarter was the first time we saw 2025 JK Dobbins, and the Broncos and this offense need to see that version of Dobbins a lot more moving forward.

RJ Harvey – Stock down: After seeing heavy usage the last few games, we barely saw the Broncos’ explosive runner on Sunday. He played just 37% of the snaps and had just 3 carries for 7 yards and 1 target for 0 catches.

Do I think this will continue? Probably not. However, this was the first game with Sean Payton calling plays this season, and we saw an increased workload for Dobbins and less work for Harvey,

Tyler Badie – Unchanged: He did not see the touches he was getting previously, but his role remained the same. He is a third-down pass-blocking back who occasionally gets some touches in the run and pass game.

Adam Prentice – Unchanged: Played just 6 snaps on offense but did see his first carry of the season.

Wide Receiver

Jaylen Waddle – Stock down: The Broncos’ big offseason addition started to show some frustration on the field on Sunday, and well, it’s warranted. He was supposed to change this offense, but once again, he was an afterthought during the game, finishing with 5 targets and 2 catches for 19 yards. He did have a costly drop late in the game, and it was simply another disappointing effort for the Broncos’ explosive pass catcher.

We need Nix and Waddle to improve their chemistry on the field, and do it quickly.

Courtland Sutton – Stock up slightly: Like Dobbins, Sutton was invisible for most of the game. However, in the 4th quarter, he showed some life and caught his first touchdown of the season. His stat line is nothing to write home about, but we need to get Sutton going and, hopefully, these signs of life lead to more consistency moving forward.

Marvin Mims Jr. – Stock up: His play as a wide receiver was lackluster, but he showed life as a returner for the first time this season and had a 27-yard punt return to set the Broncos up in good field position.

Troy Franklin – Stock up: With Pat Bryant going on the short-term IR, Franklin saw added snaps on Sunday, but it did not amount to much. Still, it appears Franklin will have a larger role in the offense until Bryant returns from an ankle injury.

Lil’Jordan Humphrey – Unchanged: He was added to the roster after Bryant was added to the IR and saw 14 snaps with the offense vs. the Chargers. LJH saw 2 targets and turned that into 1 catch for 8 yards.

Tight End

Evan Engram –Unchanged: Engram has been outsnapping Adam Trautman the past few weeks with Davis Webb calling plays, but with Payton back calling plays, both saw 30 snaps on Sunday. With that said, Engram led the team in receiving with 4 catches for 55 yards, including a 34-yard reception early on that led to the Broncos’ first-quarter touchdown.

We’ll see how this trend continues moving forward.

Adam Trautman – Unchanged: His role is what it is, and Sean Payton favors him, so he’ll keep playing.

Nate Adkins – Unchanged: Adkins played 31% of the snaps, and his role as the third tight end/blocking specialist remains unchanged.

Dallen Bentley – Unchanged: Red-shirt rookie year for the Broncos ‘ 7th-round tight end.

Offensive Line

Garett Bolles – Unchanged: The Broncos OL has struggled a bit this season, but Bolles remains solid as Nix’s blindside blocker.

Ben Powers – Stock down: I am no offensive line expert, but the Broncos have had a lot of pressure come through the middle of the line. I am not sure if it all lands on Powers, but the pressure is happening.

Luke Wattenberg – Stock down: His snaps continue to be off target from time to time, and the pressure is coming through the middle of the line.

Quinn Meinerz – Unchanged: All-Pro caliber guard.

Mike McGlinchey – Stock down: Penalties and inconsistent blocking have been a trend this season for the Broncos veteran right tackle.

Alex Palczewski – Stock up: Saw 8 snaps on offense on Sunday in heavy packages, and with the Broncos leaning on the run game more, he could see more snaps moving forward. You could also make the case that he should see time at left guard or even right tackle.

Matt Peart – Unchanged: Saw 6 snaps on special teams.

Alex Forsyth – Unchanged: Saw 6 snaps on special teams.

Kage Casey – Unchanged: Redshirt rookie year and is probably locked in the weight room.

Defensive Line

Zach Allen – Stock up: Sack, forced fumble, and continues to be one of the best overall players on the Broncos this season.

DJ Jones – Stock up: Showed some life as a pass rusher and sacked Justin Herbert

Malcolm Roach – Unchanged: Played solid from what I saw. He has been consistent all season, but I hoped we would see a little more pass rush from him.

Eyioma Uwazurike – Unchanged: Played 45% of the snaps vs. the Chargers and had a big TFL late in the game.

Sai’vion Jones – Unchanged: He was active ahead of Jordan Jackson and played 30% of the snaps but did not register a tackle.

Jordan Jackson – Stock down: Was inactive on Sunday as the Broncos decided to go with Jones instead of him.

Tyler Onyedim – Unchanged: Redshirt rookie year continues. Hopefully, we can see him get some playing time this season.

Edge rusher

Nik Bonitto – Stock up: Bonitto finally showed some life on Sunday and totaled 2 sacks vs. the Chargers’ banged-up OL and Justin Herbert. We need more of these types of performances from Bonitto moving forward.

Jonah Elliss – Unchanged: He pressured Herbert a few times, but overall, I still want more from Elliss.

Que Robinson – Stock up: His play is not perfect, but he has made more impact plays this season than Jonah Elliss. He changed the entire momentum on Sunday when he stonewalled Justin Herbert on a 4th-and-1 QB sneak. That turnover on downs led to a 13-0 run by the Broncos, who would go on to win the game.

Dondrea Tillman – Stock up: He’s in a reserve role but made a few impact plays on Sunday, including a TFL and a near sack/safety of QB Justin Herbert.

Linebacker

Alex Singleton – Stock down: I thought he was playing solid for the most part, but he then whiffed on a tackle on a key 3rd-and-15 play. If he made the tackle, it would have been 4th and short, and the Chargers would have to punt it away or attempt to go for it. However, his whiff led to a big first down and eventually the Chargers’ first touchdown.

Gotta tackle better.

Justin Strnad – Stock up: Strnad was solid vs. the Chargers and had 1 TFL and a PBU late in the game. He has been fairly consistent for the Broncos this season.

Jordan Turner – Unchanged: Played 70% of the special teams snaps.

Karene Reid – Unchanged: Played 50% of the special teams snaps.

Cornerback

Pat Surtain II – Unchanged: Escaped with just a minor ankle injury and avoided the injured reserve, but missed Sunday’s game.

Riley Moss – Unchanged: Suffered a rib injury vs. the 49ers and did not play vs. the Chargers.

Ja’Quan McMillian – Stock up: Played well and showed off his pass rush ability on the Hail Mary attempt on the final play of the game when he blitzed and sacked quarterback Justin Herbert.

Jahdae Barron – Stock up: Played 100% of the defensive snaps and looked pretty good. Again, the Chargers’ passing game was VERY limited, but he was physical in the run game and as a tackler and did not embarrass himself out there. The Seahawks present a much bigger challenge for him and the Broncos’ secondary.

Kris Abrams-Draine – Stock up: Played 100% of the snaps and, like Barron, did not disappoint. He had an INT called back due to DPI, but otherwise, KAD was solid vs. the Chargers. He will have a tougher test vs. the Seahawks on Thursday Night.

Safety

Talanoa Hufanga – Unchanged: He had a forced fumble, but would leave the game due to an injury and was ruled out. We’ll have to see if he can rebound on a short week.

Brandon Jones – Stock up: You can make the argument that he has been one of the Broncos’ better players this season. He is always around the ball and had a big INT on Justin Herbert late in the game.

Devon Key – Stock up: When Hufanga went out, Key came in and is the Broncos’ third safety. He could get a start on Thursday Night if Hufanga cannot play vs. the Seahawks.

Tycen Anderson – Unchanged: Played 80% of the special teams snaps.

JL Skinner – Stock up: Played 63% of the special teams snaps and had a few big tackles in the return game.

Special Teams

K Wil Lutz – Stock down: Went 3 for 4 on Sunday, but missed another 40 yard attempt and now has a missed FG in three straight games. Need more consistency from the Broncos’ kicker.

P Jeremy Crawshaw – Stock up: Has been very consistent this season and has flipped the field position and pinned opposing teams deep in their own territory multiple times this season.

LS Mitchell Fraboni – Unchanged: Good snaps.
